utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to greet you all. It's case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I'd like to welcome all the people present in the courtroom: Mr. Scott, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as the witness Mr. Manolic, as well as all those people present in the courtroom. The registrar, before the hearing, told me we had a technical difficulty with the transcript. The technical engineer has been working on it for the last few minutes because we're trying to boost the system. So we will have to nevertheless continue with the hearing, and if you can't read the transcript, just take notes and then you can check it out with the transcript afterwards. Before resuming the cross-examination, which ended off with Mr. Praljak taking the floor yesterday, I would like to say the following: Yesterday, we listened with great attention to the questions that were put to the witness. Personally, I didn't quite understand the meaning of some of your questions, and this morning I read the pre-trial brief of your Defence counsel that had been filed pursuant to the filing of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. In this pre-trial brief you clearly spell out what your Defence strategy is, and in its conclusion you indicate that you were innocent and that you hope that a confrontation with witnesses will enable you to render you not guilty. So you clearly stated that you were eagerly awaiting the testimony of the witnesses to clearly assess this. And on reading your submissions, I discovered that you have mentioned a number of interesting items, namely the international armed conflict and the joint criminal enterprise, and to support your arguments you quoted in your submissions a number of examples. I would just like to outline a few of these. This has been recorded, and therefore it has been made public. As far as international conflict is concerned, in paragraph 26 you drew up a list of all the things which Croatia has done. You said that Croatia has supplied the ABiH and the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina with equipment, has funded the training of a number of military units or police units that included Muslims that went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the Republic of Croatia was training helicopter pilots and tolerated military equipment transfers and convoys. So all of this is extremely interesting, and you can put this in the form of a question to the witness to corroborate what you have mentioned in your submissions, because what you've mentioned in your submissions is not supported by anything you say here. You also say that Croatian hospitals had cared for 12.000 Bosnians, which of course could be a useful element to be borne in mind by the Bench and the Defence counsel, and this could be corroborated by the witness. In addition, under exceptional circumstances we had said that you could put questions on -- on -- you could put questions on technical matters. This is why you have been entitled to ask questions of a technical nature. In paragraph 74 of your submissions, and thereafter the title is "Bosnia has attacked the Republic of Croatia," you quote a number of things that are of a military -- quite obviously -- that are quite obviously of a military nature. In paragraph 77 you explain that the Republic of Croatia deployed a new military strategy in the south of the country, and you say that in the spring of 1992 an HV battalion comprising 459 soldiers were positioned in Citluk in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the kind of useful question which you can put to the witness. The witness can confirm or deny what you're saying. You also mentioned that the HV was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they never exceeded 500. Perhaps the witness can confirm this, can say this is true or not, and so on and so forth. Mr. Praljak, you -- when you ask a question, that's all very well, but the questions need to be useful questions that serve your interests. So I've just mentioned a number of questions which you can put to the witness, and this is contained in your submissions. The witness can confirm what you are saying or can disagree with you. So you should make the most of it, because I don't know at what point in time you will be able to ask these questions again at a later stage. Yesterday, you had a book with 220 documents, or a bundle with 227 documents. I think it would be more useful to put questions on those points you have mentioned in your submissions. I hesitate to interrupt you because I don't know what your strategy is, and I don't know the reasons for which you ask these questions, but the Bench does not want the trial to last for longer than it should, and sometimes you spend a lot of time on questions which could have been put differently. You could have put the questions more specifically. Yesterday, I asked you how much time you needed, and you were unable to tell me how much time you needed. I don't want to find myself in the situation where some Trial Chambers find themselves. In other words, the Bench has to interrupt the accused and say, "This is not relevant and is not of any interest." You are entitled, of course, to a fair trial and you are entitled to put your questions to the witness, but if do so, this should be useful and the question must be relevant and must relate to the indictment and there must be a probative value in your question. If there is no relevance and no probative value, we are all wasting our time. This is something I wanted to call to your attention, Mr. Praljak, to make sure that the questions you put in the future are useful for the Bench and also useful for your own defence. And we don't want to adversely affect the other accused, because their Defence counsel also need time to speak up. I would be very happy to stay here for 25 years and address all of this in great detail. Unfortunately, we have time constraints and we can't do this. Therefore, we all -- we must all focus on what is essential and stick to the time limits. As I've told you already, if you don't have time to ask some questions, when it is time for the Defence to present its case, then you can ask questions which you were unable to ask during the Prosecution case, and at the end of the day, when your Defence counsel -- when the Defence counsel file their submissions, you can also include those questions which have not been addressed at this stage. So I think the position of the Bench is very clear. We want you to put questions, of course, but the questions must be relevant, and we don't want to have the feeling that we're wasting our time. Your submissions are perfectly relevant and relate to important points. And seize this opportunity. You have a witness here in the courtroom, and you should thereby confirm what you would like to confirm through the witness. You have the floor, Mr. Praljak, and you may ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. The whole problem with the way that the questions are being put, all of this comes from the fact that it is very difficult to comprehend this concept, joint criminal enterprise. Despite the fact that I talked to the lawyers, despite the fact that in Zagreb a body has been formed comprising law professors, including Professor Damaska, all of whom invested a lot of effort, nobody can give us as precise answer as to where the guilt lies in that concept. I know where I was and what I did, but I'm not here quite certain in where I stand. If Mr. Manolic, who was the second-ranking official in a state, is able to say that Franjo Tudjman went to Karadjordjevo and that that was a criminal act, then that makes me guilty automatically, regardless of whether I was on the ground, was not on the ground, whether I was in Paris or elsewhere. This is the reason why we are having all this difficulty with formulating our questions, Your Honour. Thank you. Now I would like to proceed with the ensuing matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karadjordjevo. That is quite a major topic. They're trying to portray it as one of the problems in the war which resulted in all these criminal activities, and this is where the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually started, because allegedly it was discussed by Tudjman and Milosevic precisely in Karadjordjevo. In the Blaskic case, in the judgement in that case, it is stated these aspirations for division were clear in confidential discussions on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina led by Tudjman and Milosevic on the 30th of March, 1991, in Karadjordjevo. Your Honours, this is a judgement of this Honourable Tribunal. They were unable to establish the accurate date. It wasn't on the 30th of March but, rather, on the 25th of March. And we are discussing a very significant crime and can't even establish the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was on the 25th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak says that in the judgement this was not specified. Mr. Praljak stated that it was on the 25th of March, and you say that it was also on the 25th of March. So everybody agrees on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want -- I'm just going to start out the day by objecting again and making it clear that we are going to -- I ask that Mr. Praljak ask specific questions to the witness. He starts off already by making -- he's made several speeches so far. I also note for the record that the Prosecution used approximately 5 hours and 20 minutes. The Chamber has said that in the absence of agreement among counsel each Defence team will get one sixth of the total time. Mr. Praljak so far has used up approximately 42 minutes of his time, so I note that, for the record, this would mean about 55 minutes for each Defence team, so the Praljak Defence now has approximately 13 minutes left, including counsel and Mr. Praljak. So perhaps Mr. Praljak would like to use his very limited time very wisely by asking questions rather than making speeches. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Mr. Praljak, you have focused on this meeting between Milosevic and Tudjman. You've highlighted this. You said that this took place on the 25th of March, 1991. Now, put your question to the witness. What is the question you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it on the 25th of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, as you can see, I'm short on time. Please just give me yes or no answers, or "I don't remember," or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manolic. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Tudjman tell you about what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle it was agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So in principle some things were agreed upon. All right. Do you know which commission was supposed to implement that agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission was established subsequently by President Tudjman. The names of the members are well known because they were announced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you believe that the commission failed to reach a solution even though two people had reached an agreement? How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret it in such a way that this division in principle was absurd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you think that Tudjman didn't know that this division was absurd before he proceeded to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did, because otherwise he wouldn't have negotiated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know, in the course of the war, how many times Tudjman and Milosevic met?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to tender some documentation to the Trial Chamber about 48 meetings of different sorts, meetings between Tudjman and Milosevic, where it can be seen what was discussed and how. Immediately after the meeting on the 25th in Karadjordjevic, was there on the 28th a meeting of all presidents in Split?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: After that meeting in Karadjordjevo, were there six meetings of all presidents of all republics?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the Defence and National Security Council, of which you were a member yourself, wrote a letter to the UN Security Council, to the presiding of the Council of EC, Mr. Willy Claes, and others, saying the following: We believe, or the Council believes that the pressure and threats advanced against Croatia are unreasonable due to following reasons: Croatia was the first country to recognise the sovereignty and integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatia still continues to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. Croatia supports the principle of territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen the letter that you mentioned, but the other facts that you are mentioning --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Manolic. You either know about the letter or you don't know about the letter. Do you know that in several interviews Franjo Tudjman said the following: "As for the rest, I repeat once and forever there was never any alleged agreement on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina between Tudjman and Milosevic." Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Slobodan Milosevic said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear to whom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: -- in the published report Tudjman told me that he wanted an independent Croatia, but we simply couldn't agree. He wanted to destroy the institutions, advisory institutions, and I could not accept that, just as previously I accepted amendments to the constitution that would allow for self-determination. There was some speculation about us agreeing on the division of Yugoslavia. Now I'm telling you, had we decided it at the time, we could have proceeded with implementation immediately. In the same letter to the Security Council, under paragraph (F), it says as follows: "The best confirmation of our viewpoints is contained in the already-advanced proposal of Croatia which we are now voicing again, namely for the UNPROFOR to conduct an efficient border control, both between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well as between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the entire border, not just the UNPA zones." Are you aware of this letter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the conversation either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Manolic, you either know, you don't know, you don't remember. Please help me complete my task. Milosevic gave the statement to Laura Silber and Allan Little. The statement by Tudjman and Milosevic in Geneva on the 17th of July, 1993. The president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, following a meeting held under the auspices of the co-presidents of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, Thorvald Stoltenberg and Lord Owen published or, rather, gave the following statement: "The speculations on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina are completely unfounded, the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia." That was paragraph one. Paragraph two: "The only way to achieve long-term peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina lies in the affirmation of the interests of all three constituent nations and achievement of agreement on establishment of three republics within a confederation." Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the statement, but I don't know about the content of the discussions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How could you know, since you were not there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to interject on this line of questions. If Mr. Praljak knows the witness wasn't there, then why is he asking him questions about it? Now, if we're going to spend -- Mr. Praljak has now used up his allotted time. The Praljak Defence had approximately 55 minutes, we've come to 55 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the question is an interesting one since the witness is being asked if Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic, in July, 1993, had made a joint statement with respect to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so this would go in favour of the idea that Croatia did not want to raise the question of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the witness is asking -- is being asked whether he knew about that joint statement and what he can say about it, his comments. So there we have it. It's an important question. So I don't understand your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem at all if the witness is asked questions, direct questions which then he can add -- respond to, but all Mr. Praljak has done the last few minutes is read from other documents and then just say, Are you aware of that document? And Mr. -- the answers over the last few minutes is Mr. Manolic says, no, I'm not aware of that particular document, or yes, I am, and then he tries to explain something to answer the very -- to give the Court the very information you just indicated, Your Honour, and he goes on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't know the document, but he does know the subject of the joint statement. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in that case, this is a follow-up question. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Praljak is not asking the follow-up question, and then he just goes on to the next document. So let Mr. Manolic give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just merely wanted to point out that yesterday the gentleman gave all sorts of opinions. Now he's being asked specific questions. It appears that he wasn't there, he doesn't know, he's unaware, so it calls into question his credibility and his veracity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to take the time, but I want to be very clear on this because I'm not trying to interfere with the proper questions being put to the witness. I understand that he can ask probing questions of the witness. I understand that fully. But simply to get up and read and refer to documents out of a book and say, Have you heard of this document, have you heard of this document, have you heard of this document? is not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. Praljak, the witness has just said that he does not know the object of the meeting, but he heard what you read out, so go ahead and ask him what the consequences were of the joint statement made by Tudjman and Milosevic, even if he is not aware of the paragraphs quoted. And you can ask follow-up questions. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, 1993, what post did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of the House of Counties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What do you know -- what happened after that statement? Following that statement, was it a period of fierce conflict between the HDZ and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That culminated in the conflict between the HVO and the Bosnian army. And I think that the context -- let me just tell you that why Milosevic sent the letter was a defence from the overall attack launched by the international community on this rumour that was going round that they were in fact partitioning Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, what could I say to that? Bosnia is divided today with all the pressures that went on, but never mind. What I want to tell the Court here is the following: When -- well, I have to ask the witness whether he knows about this, but when one of the members of the committee was questioned, which Franjo Tudjman appointed to divide that same Bosnia - and the man is Mr. Bilandzic - at the Tribunal in The Hague the Prosecutor asked the following question: "All right, Doctor, you took part in the meeting as a member of the Croatian delegation in order to deal with the question of maps and to determine which portion would go to Serbia and which portion would fall to Croatia. Is that correct?" And the answer was: "No, that is not correct." We don't have enough time, but I'd just like to tender this and say the following: Dr. Jovic, or, rather, Borislav Jovic, member of the Yugoslav state Presidency, in The Hague provided his diaries and signed to say they were authentic, and he addresses the meeting of the -- of the meeting in Karadjordjevo: Franjo Tudjman, Milosevic, Bilandzic, Babic, Jovic, Smilja Avramov; all of them address the issue of Karadjordjevic and all of them say that there was no division, so my question to you is the following: If you were opposed to the division and Franjo Tudjman's policy, why didn't you leave him then and there? Why didn't you establish a new party or join another party? Why did you agree to the criminal enterprise pursued by Mr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't leave a policy or a party because you don't agree over one issue. There are a certain -- there are a series of other issues for which I stayed on in the Croatian Democratic Union and in the leadership together with President Tudjman. There you have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Despite that, or, rather, despite the fact that that kind of policy and politics, according to the International Tribunal was condemned and an indictment raised, and it was stated that it was a criminal enterprise on the part of Franjo Tudjman against another state, that was not something that interested you at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to that question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be shown this next document on the ELMO, on the overhead projector, please, so that he can just confirm what he sees. I'm going to ask him about those documents. Mr. Manolic, when 5.000 Mujahedins entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992, and partially in 1993, you were the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia or the chief of all the secret intelligence services of the Republic of Croatia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, but I'd like to specify when I was Prime Minister and when I was the rest. The dates you mention are not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, how long were you Prime Minister of Croatia for; what period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until August, 1991. From August 1991. Until August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Up until what date in 1993 were you the head of all the secret and intelligence services of the presidential office for national security, the body that conjoined all the secret services of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of time. I can't establish which period of time. Afterwards I wasn't occupying any positions. If you have a document appointing me, then I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you in that post or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Which period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you now exactly. I can't specify because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know when you were head of the secret services of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the dates, and we're talking about dates now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know the month?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to months, yes, I can tell you that. It was round about November, from November onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Up until when?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I was elected president of the House of Counties, that is to say March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from November, 1992, to March, 1993, you were in charge of the secret services of Croatia; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the department or office of the president of the republic for intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991, not 1992. 1991. From November, 1991, until March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So November, 1991, to March, 1993, or was it November, 1992, to March, 1993, that you were occupying that function within the presidential office in charge of the secret services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 18th of November. Yes, November, 1991. From that date until March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for specifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At that time, 5.000 Mujahedin passed through Croatia on their way to Bosnia to fight on the side of the BH army. Did you prevent that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not prevented. I didn't even know about that. I didn't know about the figures you're telling us about now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, may we have the next document placed on the ELMO, please. I'm afraid you can't see it very well, but those the names of the people, and you're saying you never heard of any of those names or saw any of them. Thank you. May we have the next document, please. This is the attack by the Yugoslav People's Army and Chetniks on Croatia from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is this a correct map?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact borders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Next paper, please. Could you zoom in, please, focus better. Now, on this map -- zoom out. This map shows the bases and places in the Republic of Croatia from which weapons were taken for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent out to them. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Next piece of paper, please. That will do, Mr. Manolic. Could you please just give me yes or no answers. Leave the explanations out. I'm not asking for an explanation from you. You gave your explanations when questioned by the Prosecutor. All I wish to establish was that it was either the Prime Minister in whose government we have the minister of the interior or the chief of all the secret and intelligence services, who knows everything, suddenly knows nothing about this attack, about the Mujahedin. So just tell me "yes," "no," or "I don't know." Now, here --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I say something? When I started my testimony, I said at the time that I would be testifying about the facts that I am aware of and know about either directly or from certain sessions and meetings that I attended. Everything that you're asking me now and putting to me now are things that were not discussed at any of the meetings that I took part in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here in this text we see the establishment of military offices and departments of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - that's what it says here on this piece of paper - in the Republic of Croatia in July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me. I wonder, do we have the English translation of this document? And I don't know if any of the documents have been provided in cross-examination. I think the Court ruled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we don't seem to have the English translation, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have, and it is actually in the e-court under number 3D 120023. And we have the binders here, and also for the Judges, and if we can now distribute it, it will be fine. We were planning to distribute when I would be starting, but is probably a better time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have the e version in English. May we see it come up on our screens, please, Mr. Registrar. So the document does exist in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I have to make a correction. I was reading the number for the page. Actually the number of this document is 3D 00302.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, what I want to do is to show quite clearly through my questions that in Croatia, with respect to this document, during the clash between the BH army and the HVO, Franjo Tudjman, who hated Muslims, who divided Bosnia, allowed the formation of these offices or, rather, departments of the Main Staff of the army fighting with part of his people in the HVO. Did you know about this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those outposts are always established precisely in the aim of establishing more efficient cooperation between the enemy forces and one's own forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, maybe. I've never heard that in my life before. But the HVO cooperated with Goering, Goebbels, Heitel, or whoever else in the sense of better cooperation with enemy forces, and then supplied them with weapons to attack the French, I don't know about that, but anyway, thank you. Next document, please. This is a similar document. It's also about armed forces of the BH army on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Do you know of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is also in your folder and it is in e-court 3D 00186.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, excuse me. Two things, important points. I think it was the Trial Chamber's earlier ruling that all the materials for cross-examination should be provided to the Prosecution prior to the beginning, at the end of direct examination. Also -- which I don't think has been done, as far as I can tell. Secondly, I understand that Mr. Praljak is a layperson, but nonetheless if he is going to participate in the process in this way, then he needs to proceed in a proper way and give us exhibit numbers and document numbers. It's the only way we can have a record and know what's being referred to. It could very well be, Your Honour, it would be much more effective for counsel, for Mr. Kovacic to conduct such an examination along the lines that it's legally done, but Mr. Praljak, if he's going to stand up and talk about exhibits and documents, he's going to have to give us exhibit numbers, the English translations are going to have to come up. We have to be able to proceed in a reasonable way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, as far as possible please give us the numbers of the documents so that the Prosecution can access them and to help the Judges to go straight to the documents. But, Mr. Kovacic has just intervened to tell us the number of the map, has he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all with respect to the comment made from the opposite side, all the documents were released yesterday through e-court at the end of the examination-in-chief, provided to the Prosecution, a whole set which we might either use or not use, but we provided the whole set. We supplied Your Honours with the same package in the hard copy version, physically in the folders. Since it's difficult to coordinate, I suggest that when Mr. Praljak mentions a document, we shall officially tender it and give you the numbers, but they are accessible to one and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now, Mr. Scott, apparently you do have the documents that the witness -- that Mr. Praljak is putting to the witness. They were communicated to you yesterday through e-court. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... apparently what happened is the way the e-court system works is that documents can be "released," but that just simply means that there is a bunch of documents in the system. There is no identification that these are the documents that are going to be used tomorrow for the cross-examination of this witness, there's just a universe of documents. So I think -- the Prosecution, Your Honour, has to provide a list of exhibit numbers, a list of exhibits to be used in examining the witness, I think the Defence should be required to do the same thing so that we know what documents are coming up. If they say they're in e-court, there's thousands of documents in e-court. We don't know which documents they're going use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, up to now it has been the rule, and I think that the problem my learned friend is raising is simply something he has constructed now, because Your Honour said that if in seven hours the Prosecutor finishes his direct, at seven -- after seven hours and one minute, put into the system the documents you will use tomorrow, and this is precisely what we did yesterday. One or two minutes after the end of the direct, we released the documents. I know what the problem is because we have the same problem. There are very many documents in e-court now, so it's very hard for the Prosecutor to monitor this. But there is a way in which he can technically establish which document we released at that time. Whether they know this or not, that's their problem. If the Prosecutor - I'm not sure I understood - is saying that we should also provide a written list, Your Honours, I don't have the resources for that, or the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine. But when you put the system into the -- into e-court, what stops you to do what the Prosecution does, to make a chart with exhibits for Prosecution witness Josip Manolic? You could follow the same example. [In English]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Exhibit for Defence, cross-examination, and then you could put Manolic with a list of documents. In that way, the Prosecution, at 7.01 minutes, will know that these are the documents to be used. So it will suffice if your assistants make a recapitulation or summary of the texts, and the Prosecution will know that you might choose to present one of those documents during your cross-examination so that we have a parallel system between the two parties, because when you come to have your own Defence witnesses, you're going to have to have the same list, just like the Prosecutor, because it's out of the question for the Judges to come up with dozens of documents when a witness arrives without having a list beforehand. So it's always good to have a summary list of all the documents. It's not a complicated procedure, and please try and do that, would you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have such a list for our internal use, and I can provide it right now if it will assist my learned friends. I only wish to remind the Court that because we have a new system, we are all establishing new rules, and Your Honours are providing new rules from time to time, and of course we are willing to adapt to these. But let me just say that the objection raised by the Prosecutor is out of place because up to now we have respected the rules that were in place. Would the usher please hand this to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So we've already seen this map. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I observe, Your Honours, during the direct examination things turn up which simply cannot be foreseen, and I'm unable to communicate with my counsel between the direct examination and what has to be said. That's why these things happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I apologise for interrupting, but you're telling me something that I hadn't realised up until now. Do you want to say that you were not in contact with your lawyer before the examination-in-chief? I don't know what time your lawyers are here, what time they start in the morning, but if they come in before the sitting begins, you can discussion this with them. The Defence counsel can discuss how the day is going to evolve with their client, how they envisage the day, because I assume that the accused turn up at least half an hour before the morning sitting. So if the counsel arrive half an hour before, they will have ample time to consult their clients, will they not? But anyway, that's a problem that should be addressed and that you have. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we appreciate your interest. We hope that Your Honour will make it possible for us to have regular contact with our clients, and we really respect Your Honour's efforts, especially because of that Friday problem we mentioned. We do have 15 or 20 minutes in the morning before the hearing, and sometimes we even manage to get five or ten minutes after the session, and during breaks in the course of the day. However, very often, yes, this is enough because we only have a few issues to raise. However, when we are discussing matters such as joint criminal enterprise and potentially thousands of documents, there's simply not enough time to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But if we bear that in mind, I thought that Friday was a good day for the accused to meet their lawyers, to look at the debriefing of the previous week and the coming week and to prepare for the cross-examination in the coming week. I know you have to meet with your clients, otherwise there is going to be problems. But anyway, Mr. Praljak, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, this map shows the training centres in the Republic of Croatia where members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were trained in 1991 and 1992. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now for the next document, please. Thank you. On this map we see the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were established on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in 1992. Do you know anything about this and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not enter into the activities of the army, the minister of defence, and the army staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mean the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with the knowledge and assistance of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, please. Are you aware of the training centres in the Republic of Croatia in which pilots of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were trained in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next document, please. This document contains a list of pilots of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were trained on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Of course, with the knowledge of the minister of the defence, the president, Franjo Tudjman. I had hoped that you would know something about it too. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... without an exhibit number, we cannot pull it up in e-court, so we renew our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, this list of pilots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously -- excuse me. The two previously mentioned documents are numbers 3D 00313 and 3D 00314. This document, however, is not in the database, and we will tender it separately. For now it's only used for purposes of putting the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it doesn't have a number. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we have the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think that will be tendered as an exhibit. This is merely a tool to enhance the memory and to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no -- then there's absolutely no foundation. We don't even know if this thing is accurate or if this is something Mr. Praljak made up last night. I don't know where it came from or what it's for if it's not offered for the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I propose that the Prosecutor have a little patience and Mr. Praljak will say where this information comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that these hospitals shown here took care of wounded soldiers and civilians of Muslim ethnicity in 1992 up until 1995? The hospitals of Split-Firule, Split-Krizine, Split-Toplice, Zagreb, Karlovac, Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci, Metkovic. I wish to mention to Your Honours and Mr. Scott that there are documents about every single patient treated in these hospitals. I just want to ask whether Mr. Manolic knows about these hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I think you're putting your questions to the wrong witness. I cannot know anything about this, and you know that the minister of health of Croatia and the people working in the medical corps can certainly confirm this with certainty. So why are you putting this to me when you know in advance I had nothing to do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will finish with this line of questioning and take this map away. Mr. Manolic, it was my intention to ask you whether you have any explanation for the fact that on the one hand a person who hates Muslims - these are your words - Franjo Tudjman, who colludes with Milosevic to partition Bosnia, is doing all these things we have seen now which you have confirmed in a way.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything is possible in certain conditions. You can be treating imprisoned prisoners of war of the other side, provide humanitarian assistance. All that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Weapons, pilots?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different matter. That was the dual policy that was pursued by Milosevic and Tudjman. It was a dual policy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time the referendum was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a precondition for the work of the Badinter Commission for the gaining of independence, Croatia was a recognised state within its AVNOJ borders. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At that same time, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina held approximately 70 per cent of the territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and it was Stjepan Kljuic who told us so before this Court, a politician you hold in high regard - had for centuries aspired to accede to Croatia - these are the words of Mr. Kljuic - and live in the same state. Do you share Mr. Kljuic's opinion that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina desired to live in the same state with the Croats in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite natural. It's quite natural that they should lean towards their mother country. It's not something recent. For 40 years the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially Herzegovina, were oriented towards Croatia, including many of your friends who came to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And me, too, yes. Franjo Tudjman, as you say, agreed on the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina with Milosevic in Karadjordjevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I said that they negotiated about the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the same time you say that Franjo Tudjman hated the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I used the verb "to hate." I said he was of an anti-Muslim orientation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree that had -- that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina obeyed Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 99 per cent of the Croats voted at the referendum for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although they disagreed with the question put at the referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But tell me why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please. Based on the results of the referendum, the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Croatia recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was one of the first states to do so.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman appointed Ambassador Sancevic, and Croatia was among the first countries to appoint an ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the date. Could you remind me, please? I think it was a little later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The Croats didn't want Bosnia and Herzegovina, Franjo Tudjman wanted to partition Bosnia and Herzegovina, he reached an agreement in principle with Milosevic, and then, out of the blue, he tells the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina go and vote at the referendum, vote yes, make it possible for Bosnia-Herzegovina to survive. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony, I stated that the question of the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina was very significant in the relations between the State of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. You explain to me why this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But you said that Franjo Tudjman had authority and that the Croats, who didn't want something, obeyed him anyway. At the same time, we have to accept the fact that he didn't like the Muslims, that he wanted to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that this partition led to crimes through a series of incredible steps for which I'm being held responsible. This is what we are talking about, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again we have just a speech, Your Honour. I'm going to object to that. He can put questions to the witness. There was a fair question a moment ago. He asked Mr. Manolic to explain something and then Mr. Manolic in fact tried to give an explanation. That was a proper question, but now again we're back to speeches.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't concluded with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, no, no. We may not continue. We have to press on. Mate Granic was the minister of foreign affairs in the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in my cabinet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. In his book he stated explicitly that Alija Izetbegovic on two occasions offered to Franjo Tudjman to have the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the south of Prozor and Rama to be annexed to Croatia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You claimed that all Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina should have been taken care of; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the Washington Agreement, did the Muslims and Croats jointly receive 51 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What happened with the Croats who lived beyond, outside of this territory, if you were so pleased with the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following this, a second agreement ensued.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that. After the Washington Agreement, the conflict between the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina ceased; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the greatest achievement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How was it possible, then, in the situation where there was no further conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was no Mate Boban any longer, the international community was pressing for peace, so please explain then to us the continued attacks on Sarajevo, the massacre in Srebrenica and Zepa, and Bihac, which was saved by the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me now about the things that I know of only from the press, just like you do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Up until March of 1993, you were chief of all secret services. You were also the speaker of the Upper House of the Croatian parliament. That's a fact. Did you know of the existence of collection centres in Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Based on what do you think that President Tudjman knew about these collection centres in Gabela when you yourself, despite your high office, knew nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had direct contact with the military leadership, and all of this was in the hands of military, so no other government officials had to be involved in this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You continued as member of the Defence and National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You were still a high-ranking member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You had contact with the HDZ members of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question that you are putting was never raised at any meetings of Defence and National Security Council. The camps were never discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that every little person knew about these collection centres, every little person in Croatia knew about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you were not just some little person, and you knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing is to know, another thing is to participate in this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We're not talking about participation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can know certain things from the press. You can hear rumours, but that doesn't mean that you're taking any part in decision-making, and that was my situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, nobody says here that you were the decision-maker. You said that every little person or every little policeman in Croatia knew about the existence of these collection centres, whereas you, who were the top-ranking policeman in Croatia, say that you knew nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew nothing of it. In my evidence, I said that the International Red Cross Committee visited these centres and it was then that it was made somewhat known to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you about this before the visit of the International Red Cross or after?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that this took place somewhat later, in 1993. Could you please give me the specific time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Your human, professional, and moral, and political duty -- was it your human, professional, moral and political duty, you as member of the Upper House of Croatian parliament, were you duty-bound to bring this up in any of the sessions? Should you have banged your hand on the table and said to Franjo Tudjman, "This may not continue"? Wasn't it your duty to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Praljak. When this was made public, it was only then that it was discussed at a session of Defence and National Security Council and it was then that Minister Granic brought this up, this discussion, but this was towards the end, and the discussion was to disband these camps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that Minister Granic intervened only when it was announced on television, because one of the people who were accused for creating these camps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go more slowly. The interpreters are finding it -- finding it difficult to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should put that question to Minister Granic about when he intervened, when he got involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you were Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia, the Croatian Party of Rights established its own armed forces, Croatian armed forces known as HOS.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illegal paramilitary declared to be paramilitary by the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. All correct. Did these forces seize a building in the centre of Zagreb, a building known as Starcevic Centre, and did they install an anti-aircraft gun in that building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I'm aware of that because I took part in resolving that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did Prime Minister -- or was Prime Minister Josip Manolic duty-bound to act in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How long did they remain there before you intervened and acted in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. If you know the dates, then please go ahead and give them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did these armed forces have their military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did they have their generals?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the generals because they -- nobody was given that rank until much later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You would then agree that for months you failed to resolve a crisis. This was actually a military coup in the capital city, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we didn't want to resolve it. At the time, Croatian authorities, led by the Prime Minister and president of the state, were not interested in the showdown with a faction that portrayed itself as Greater Croatian force. We found another way which proved to be much more efficient than these military police measures that you seem to propose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you can't know what I am thinking of, what's in my mind. I just asked you about what steps you had taken. We cannot imagine something like this taking place either in London or in Paris. Something like this could have happened only because this was such a young [Realtime transcript read in error "long"] state, so powerless and faced with so many problems that even something as obvious or as blatant as a military putsch in the middle of Zagreb they failed to resolve; isn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear, but I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please go ahead then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow me to interrupt. Mr. Praljak said that there was a military coup. Is this something you agree with or which you deny?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't confirm that this was a military coup, because it would have had to produce some consequences which would normally entail a change in the ruling structures, and there was nothing of the sort. With time we took some steps against these people who were working to undermine the government of the sovereign Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was General Spegelj accused by federal authorities for the violation of the constitutions of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such accusations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did the federal government indict Franjo Tudjman because he had written a letter to the US president, Bush Senior?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know about the letter, and I also don't know about any indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a collective body?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the president of the Presidency automatically commander-in-chief of the armed forces of the SFRY, Supreme Commander of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did Stipe Mesic become president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be specific with the date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was Stipe Mesic president of the Presidency of the SFRY during the attack of the JNA on Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he was against it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please. Please let me continue. Was Stipe Mesic president of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the attack of the JNA against Croatia and Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Formally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, formally speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware that Stipe Mesic, the commander-in-chief of the JNA at the time, ever wrote an order to the General Staff of the JNA whereby he would order a cessation of the attack against Slovenia and Croatia and order that the military be returned to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are meanly putting a very unilateral question. I think that it is well known that Stipe Mesic was against the escalation of the situation with the conflict with the JNA and in Slovenia. Everybody knows about the trip that he undertook at the time, and you can clarify with -- this with him further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know about him writing any order?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't know about that because that is part of internal communication of the commander-in-chief with people who are his subordinates. Please don't try to draw me into something that I know nothing about just like you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Manolic, does Croatia have more than 4 million people living outside of its borders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never counted them, but based on some writings, some writings appearing in various scientific and non-scientific publications, I think that this is the figure that is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the beginning of the independence of Croatia, during the beginning of the aggression against Croatia, did these people assist with the money? Did they provide financial assistance to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Or, rather, to Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're splitting hairs now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In percentages, was the largest number of refugees those who left due to political or economic reasons from Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, especially the immigration that started in '45.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, after the partisans imposed their laws.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no court, no laws, providing that you were not on the same side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you spoke here yesterday about how costly the funding of the HVO was for Croatia. Once you mentioned a figure of billion dollars, and one of billion Deutschmarks. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I gave an analysis. I said that that was an approximation. I said that it wasn't based on any scientific figures. The only basis was the manpower of the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you at any time require from the HVO staff to inform you about how many people they had?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because you know that at the time I was already in the opposition, and you know very well that there was no communication between the opposition parties and the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you didn't join the opposition until 1994.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is when I did this analysis. Please try to be specific with the dates, because only then can we be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. And the HVO existed already in 1991, 1992, 1993, and -- 1993. And I guess the people down there knew how many soldiers there were in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You doubt that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you provide this analysis to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which analysis? This is the analysis I gave in my book, and this is the analysis that I adhere to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how much money poured into Croatia from political and economic emigres from Bosnia and Herzegovina? This money was intended to finance the defence of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina from any aggressor regardless of who the aggressor was. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You don't know about this either. You can only speculate about this, because this -- this inflow of money from abroad, from our emigres, was completely beyond control, and this is why some criminal acts were perpetrated in that field, but that's not what we're discussing here before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, do you know that I, just like tens of thousands of others, went to Sunja near Sisak as a volunteer, violating federal laws by doing so. I went there with a rifle in order to defend. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, please, would you tell the Chamber this: Do you know, be it directly or indirectly, of any piece of information or any fact about me that you could use to testify that I in any way did or failed to do or that I instigated others to do something that can be considered criminal under any laws?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your patience. I regret that we found ourselves here facing each other as opponents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me this time. I would prefer to remain silent if it were possible. I would try to be silent as often as possible unless I'm sure that some things can be clarified only if I put questions to the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. It is now 10.30. Mr. Scott, I assume you would like to mention your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour, whenever the Court would like to do that, now or later. I'm primarily pointing out -- I want to point out a couple of things now in terms of timing and scheduling. First of all, Your Honour, I understand that the Appeals Chamber has affirmed the ruling, the Trial Chamber's ruling about the limits on cross-examination, indicating that it should be the same time as direct examination. The Appeals Chamber has issued its ruling affirming the Trial Chamber. In that regard, Your Honour, I note that, based on that ruling, based on the Trial Chamber's prior announced ruling as affirmed by the Appeals Chamber, each of the Defence teams for this witness should be allowed approximately 55 minutes. Mr. Praljak has now taken an hour and a half, so all of the Praljak Defence time has now been used and Mr. Praljak is now using the time of other Defence teams. So I would assume that other Defence teams want to have some time to question the witness as well. So perhaps they want to take that into account. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President, the way I read the initial ruling by the Court, first of all there was some flexibility built in where witnesses come in and mention particular individuals. This gentleman here has mentioned my client, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, as well as Mr. Petkovic. So in light of that and in light of the Court's ruling, I don't see why on earth we would not be given the necessary time. I also indicated yesterday the way the Prosecution is presenting its case, it's deliberately doing so in a way to obstruct justice. They're doing so because they're afraid of the truth. They don't want the truth --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Your Honour. I'm not -- that's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- that's why I'm entitled to make my record. The gentleman, in my opinion, is pursuing in an unethical manner. He's putting in all of these documents one sentence at a time, half a sentence, and then he's asking you, Your Honours, to deny us the opportunity to confront this evidence. Maybe that's what -- that's the way it's done in some fascist state. It shouldn't be done in this International Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I state the strongest possible objection. Now look at the record, Your Honour. Look what I -- Mr. Karnavas has just accused me, accused Ken Scott, professional, he's accused me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- of obstructing justice --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- and acting unethically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Those are serious allegations. I would like to know -- I think that's improper. If he has grounds for those serious allegations, he should make them known, but do not come into court and accuse me of obstructing justice and acting unethically. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How can I possibly confront all of the evidence that he's putting in, at the same time he's saying he's here for the truth? If he's here for the truth, let me get to the truth. What is he afraid of? Why read half of a sentence? That's what I call obstructing of justice. Obstructing -- we're here to get to the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and all I want to do is get to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, nobody is obstructing justice, because you know full well that the obstruction of justice amounts to contempt of court. So it's in nobody's minds that anybody would like to do such a thing. So please calm down, all of you. The question that remains is how much time is left. Seemingly the Appeals Chamber has confirmed the ruling on the time limits of the cross-examination. I have not read this yet because it has been recorded this morning. We shall read this. All we know, as far as this witness is concerned, we have spent an hour and a half this morning questioning this witness, and three hours this afternoon, so we have four and a half hours left. And we also have tomorrow. Tomorrow we will have another four hours. If -- I do not include the break time. So four hours, plus three, plus an hour and a half, we still have eight and a half hours. In that time I think a lot can be said by some of you. Mr. Praljak has addressed some of the issues, and unless you feel it is particularly useful, the other Defence counsel don't have to cover the same ground. So you have eight and a half hours left. The Prosecution has only had five hours and 25 minutes, I believe, and since yesterday we have spent or dedicated approximately three hours to the cross-examination, so in eight and a half hours you should be able to conclude the cross-examination if you are sufficiently disciplined. I trust you are able to do this. The Trial Chamber, of course, is prepared to be flexible so that all and everyone is happy and that you don't feel that the certain problems are not being addressed. During cross-examination a lot of points are mentioned, and it is very useful, so make sure you focus on what is important and what is useful to the Chamber. We shall now have a break. It is 35 minutes past 10.00, and we shall resume again at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Two observations to begin with: First of all, I invite the Defence counsel and accused not to make any personal attacks on the representatives of the OTP who are doing their job. If the job is not done properly, then it is up to the Judges to decide. So the Prosecution is putting forward a thesis. You can criticise it, but you can criticise what they're putting forward, not the person putting it forward. So no personal observations. They are misplaced in the courtroom. They don't serve any purpose. We are professional Judges, and are quite able to appreciate arguments put forward from both sides. So there's no point in hurling accusations on the one side or the other because it is up to us to decide and rule on all the things put forward relevant to the indictment. So I'd like to bring that to your attention in order to have the proceedings evolve in the best possible spirit. Now, the second point is since the Appeals Chamber rendered a decision that confirms our previous decisions and that pursuant to Article 90(F) it is the Chamber that has the discretionary right as to how much time it is going to allot to the Defence.
