So the general rule is that the Defence has the same time as the Prosecution and that in certain cases you can share the time, but as the Appeals Chamber has ruled, we invited on several occasions the lawyers to get together amongst themselves so that collectively they can designate one among their member to conduct the cross-examination in a general manner and that the others can step in if the need arises. And as I have said on numerous occasions, there's no point in you all getting up to raise the same points. So you have this collective assignment and job. Although you might not agree amongst yourselves, you should nonetheless decide upon the general points that you agree upon so that the person conducting the cross-examination on behalf of all the rest of you can ask general questions. And when the time comes and one comes to personal responsibility of your individual clients, then if a witness has not named any of the accused, the question doesn't arise. But if the witness does name names, then it is logical for the Defence counsel of that particular accused or accused can intervene on their behalf. So it is up to you to exert discipline on both sides, and it is up to you to see which one of you is going to conduct the cross-examination on the general points and then we come to the individuals where you can speak for your client, if that occasion arises, if a document is discussed which contains the name of your client, of one of the accused. But, if not, then stick to the time division and, as the Appeals Chamber has stated, one must not forget that we always have time constraints and resources and their constraints. So unfortunately, we don't have all the time in the world. I don't think that there will be any problems if you work collectively for the time being, work together in order to determine who is going to conduct the principal cross-examination of the witness. If you can't do that, then we fall back on the rule that the Appeals Chamber has put forward whereas the time is divided by six. But we should like to be more flexible. I don't want you to have the impression that we're cutting you off, but it's up to you to be more disciplined. If you cannot agree amongst yourselves, then tell us, or you cannot agree on certain points, and then you can take the floor individually when it concerns your particular client. Now, as far as this witness is concerned, I have to say that we're going to finish with the witness tomorrow at 1.45. That should be borne in mind. And also, you should bear in mind that we must leave some time for additional questions from the Prosecution, if they need to ask them, which means that you have more than eight hours at your disposal, and eight hours is a long time. A lot can be done in eight hours. Having said that, I'm going to give the floor to the next Defence counsel. I think it was Mr. Kovacic who wanted to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not going to take too much time about -- in telling you what the Defence has agreed upon, but we're all fully conscious of what we're facing and the situation we have in hand. You have explained it to us, and I think that we'll be able to get through it in the time at our disposal. Before I begin the cross-examination, just a correction: On page 36 of the transcript, line 4, it should state the "young state" and what it reads is "long." So "young," not "long." Could that be corrected, please, for the record. And, Your Honour, to draw your attention to another matter, in the viva voce witness table which we received from the OTP with the pre-trial brief, that was compiled partially following your ruling of the 13th of November, it states that witness Josip Manolic was appointed as witness -- was designated as Witness M at the time, and that that is related to the accused Slobodan Praljak. I don't see why, personally, but that's what it says on this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, having said that, let me say good afternoon, to you, Mr. Manolic. My name is Bozidar Kovacic, I am an attorney from the island of Krk, and I'm going to ask you to make pauses between question and answer, because the two of us speak the same language and of course it's natural for us to react to one another's questions and answers straight away, I to your answers, you to my questions, but please bear in mind that everything has to be interpreted which means that there's a little time that has to be left for the interpreters to do their job, so please make pauses between question and answer. Thank you. Mr. Manolic, I'd just like to try and clear up a general matter on the basis of what we have heard here for the past two days from you. I am fully convinced you will agree that this emanates from your statement that the Republic of Croatia, when it became independent and when it was being created in 1990, had the right, in the sense of the right and duty, and the moral duty as well, to bear in mind and take into consideration the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina within the context of the disintegration of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All parties, more or less, and all the political players, if I can use that term, agreed on that point. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And can we also agree that at that time, that is to say the disintegration of Yugoslavia and the creation of a new Croatia and new relationships in all the former federal republics, that the intentions of the Republic of Croatia and its political leadership - that is who I mean first of all - were very honest, proper, and morally correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In a way, from what you have told us in your answers, it would appear that in your judgement and according to your political convictions certain errors were committed in that politics and in those policies waged with the development of events and situation and that the late President Franjo Tudjman, once again, in your opinion, opted for some wrong political solutions or opted for a different approach to the approach you thought was proper. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that my whole testimony about all this period shows that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. And moreover, you specified and told us the issues over which you disagreed with him. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And one of those issues was a definition of Croatian politics towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, and policies towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that same time and in that same process and those same developments - and I'm going to try and give you the other side of the medal, if you like, put forward other elements - would you agree with me when I say that it was clear already sometime in 1991, immediately after Serbia's aggression against Croatia, that the same thing would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina? When I say is it clear, I mean not only to the political leadership but to the people as well.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to differentiate between Serbia's aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina - that's one question - it's another question the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not assume the second at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm sure you'll agree that with the development of events from 1990 to 1991, we already have the aggression against Croatia, that at a certain point in time during that process in that period, and it was a dialectic process, quite obviously, that it became clear to one and all - not only to the politicians but to everybody - that the very next day in the coming period - and that's what indeed happened - the former JNA or, rather, the military force under Serbia's control, would make certain moves and undertake occupation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but under rather different circumstances. It was aggressive towards Croatia with a help from part of the rebels, whereas in Bosnia-Herzegovina the majority of this action and operation was led by a faction, a Karadzic faction, the rebel Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes, we can agree there. But regardless of the structure, let's call it the aggressive forces, the fact remains that the war and the aggression and the persecution and all the ugly things that accompany a war happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it could have been foreseen and predicted in advance.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the aggression of the rebel Serbs could have been predicted and foreseen, but at that point in time in 1990 we couldn't have assumed that there would be a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about that first conflict, the aggression. And when that aggression on the Serb side, the Serb aggression started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, very soon after that you received information -- they were more or less public and I assume that you in the top political echelons might have been better informed than the other citizens, but it was common knowledge and generally known that people were suffering, and the Serb aggression that we're talking about specifically caused suffering, victims, refugees of both the other ethnic groups, both the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Hungarians, all other non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All the other people living there. But when we're talking about the numbers, then the prime victims were the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, with the development of events, that is to say from 1991 onwards, the Croats and the Muslims in most areas, or in all areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, began to organise themselves in a defence and tried to defend themselves in one way or another from that Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Greater Serb aggression. Now, when I say "Greater Serb," I don't mean the Serb people but an overall Greater Serbian policy of conquering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad we agree on that. So the primary victims, and they were the Muslims and the Croats, started to organise themselves and started to defend themselves from that Greater Serbian aggression. We agree on that score, do we?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, at that same time, with the developments of the situation, all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the ethnic groups, tried in one way or another to define their own positions for a future Bosnia-Herzegovina when one fine day it manages to defend itself and when war comes to an end - and of course all people think along those lines - they said they want to know why they were going to war. We Croats and we Muslims and the other ethnic groups want to know why we are fighting and what position we can expect or what situation we can expect in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Quite normal. However, the fact is that at that same time, with the Greater Serbian aggression starting, with the war starting, the first victims are visible, they are increasing from one day to the next, and at the same time, simultaneously with all that, the Croats, as the smallest ethnic group of those three large ethnic groups, had no guarantees whatsoever from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their political leaders and administrative leaders, were given no guarantees whatsoever of what they could expect in future; some sort of Serboslavia, or some dominant Muslim state, or yet again rights of a minority nation or the rights that they had from the 1974 constitution as a constituent peoples. They did not know what to expect, and the Muslim leadership or, rather, the Muslim part of the leadership, through talks and negotiations, did not wish to tell them firmly and to promise them what their situation would be: That is what your position will be if you want to fight for it. Do you agree that the Croats in Bosnia in 1991, 1992, and through subsequent talks and negotiations were never given firm assurances and promises from the other side, from their partners, if I can use that term, because they were still defending themselves together, never given those assurances and promises about what their position would be in the Bosnia and Herzegovina of the future?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are not quite right there, because contacts and communication did take place between the Presidency of the Croatian state and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I attended one such meeting in Sarajevo where these relations were still quite correct and proper. I'm referring to the relations between the Croats and the Muslims. So when we mention these first attempts of ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina to organise, we all welcomed the fact that these ethnic groups were rallying, because we knew that only if they were organised could they fight against the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with that. But the further things developed and the more talks were held, and there were talks between representatives of Croats and Muslims in Bosnia, and even the Serb side participated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what side participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- but it's a fact, and I'm telling you this as my assessment which you can either deny or agree with or partly challenge, the fact is that the public impression, the impression that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina had was that their political leadership of the time, that is the political leadership of the Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, was not giving them any promises or guarantees as to their status in the future Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe you will agree with me there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not fully. I attended talks between President Tudjman and Izetbegovic on one occasion, and Izetbegovic, as the representative of the Muslims and the Bosnian state, asked that Mr. Boban, a prominent personage in the Croatian ranks, be the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is contrary to what the other side -- I mean those holding different opinions than mine, they frequently forget this. But to clarify things, let me tell you what the response was to Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. We haven't arrived at that point in time yet. The talks you mentioned where Izetbegovic generously offered Boban the position of minister of defence, that's already far into 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Far into 1993. So this is already a time when there were attempts at reconciliation after the conflict had already broken out. So these are attempts to remedy the situation. But we're now talking about an earlier stage. I think we will agree, in view of the time we are referring to now, that the Croats were not given any clear guarantees as to their status. To put things simply, as the common people were able to understand it, Izetbegovic was sending the wrong messages. They saw that the state was not functioning, that they were not being given any promises. They see even that Croatia is wavering in its assistance, so objectively --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're back to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic is arguing his case. He's making his closing argument today. These are not questions. Look at the transcript and see. It's Mr. Kovacic stating his case, making his arguments, and these are not questions for the witness. They're also overcharacterised. How can this witness say what every Croat living in Bosnia-Herzegovina thought or what their impression was? So I object on both grounds; it's improper form and it also calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Kovacic, you are putting forward a thesis rather than taking it through question form, asking questions, which are interesting for you and the answers to which can be useful to the Judges, because you have already stated your thesis and will be able to do so subsequently and it's not up to the witness to say yes you're right or you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. I just wish to point out to the Court that, in view of the office held by the witness, he was a person with political experience and a person who is well-informed. He is therefore in a position to evaluate whether these theses are grounded in fact or not. That's why I put this question. But as for the technology, I do have the right to put my case to the witness. I will, however, do it in a simpler way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, not to weary all other parties, I think we do understand one another. Would you agree that evidently -- we cannot quantify this, but evidently a number of people, Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that situation understood that they were not being promised any kind of security by anyone in any future system?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims couldn't expect security either. This was a creation in those first few months of 1991 where in Bosnia-Herzegovina nobody could be certain about their future. None of these ethnic groups had any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I fully agree with you. And we have seen to what this uncertainty led. There was no firm alliance between the Muslims and the Croats against the Greater Serbian aggression. We saw in the period that followed, in late 1992 and in 1993, that both Muslims and Croats had terrible casualties, a lot of victims because they didn't manage to organise in time.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but you have skipped over a period in which the Croats and the Muslims did oppose the Serbian aggression at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've skipped over that and moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not to go into further details, because they no longer trusted each other, because they no longer had any promises about their future, the alliance was not strong enough. That's my case.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The very fact that the alliance fell apart goes to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, would you agree that throughout all these events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the extent you followed them, and I assume you were better informed than the ordinary citizen, would you agree that the man in the street, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, was not interested in global politics or in political or legal theories about the rights of nations and the changes to borders and so on? Would you agree that the common people, and you did have contacts with ordinary people, were interested in survival? They simply wanted to know how they could survive in this complex wartime situation. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree that that's what the man in the street was interested in. But this man in the street also realised that he had to take into account what would happen next, and this prompted them to organise and to rally round their ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. We agree fully. That's precisely my thesis. At one point, starting on the 18th of November, 1991, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, and we can see from the transcripts that it emerged as a kind of parallel organisation in parallel to the HDZ party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that formally the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established on the 18th of November, 1991, and sometime later in 1992 it began to take root and come to life, and you were monitoring the situation at the Defence and National Security Council, you understood, as did some others, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was actually becoming a parallel organisation, parallel to the party organisation. So first the Croats had been united, most of them in Bosnia and Herzegovina within the HDZ as a political movement and party, and now they were organising in a different way, in a firmer form, and this was parallel, and you discussed this at the Defence and National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it as parallelism. On the contrary. I felt that it was the HDZ that had mobilised and created the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So it can't be defined as a parallel institution. It can, rather, be defined as a joint action. The organiser was the HDZ, and it was created as a structure which the HDZ, as a political organisation, created with a view to its being transformed into something else, into a state structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you will agree, regardless of the putative goal that you mentioned, that this was aimed at strengthening defence precisely because there were no promises or guarantees for the future.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no one who could have given them any promises. You know how the international community was involved in solving these problems, and you saw that there were different combinations, different agreements, different ideas about how a peaceful solution could be reached in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct, but without quoting precisely from the record, but you have now given me an idea, President Tudjman more than once, I'm sure I saw it at least on two -- in two places in the transcripts, and I'm paraphrasing now, President Tudjman said that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in view of its complexity, will not be solved by either the Muslims or the Croats or the Serbs but by the international community, and that was constantly his position. Would you agree that he said that more than once?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said more than once that the influence of the international community could be decisive in the search for a solution in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a politician at that time, would you agree that the international community did not undertake anything that we all expected it to, maybe with too much optimism?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't use the word "nothing." I wouldn't say they didn't do anything. They were actively seeking a solution, but the complexity of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was such that the international factors found it very difficult to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on to a different topic. Maybe just two or three short questions for the sake of the Chamber. I don't believe we disagree here, so could you please keep your answers brief and just say yes or no so we could move on quickly. You told us you were one of the founders of the HDZ in Croatia. That's the transcript of the 3rd of July, the first day of your testimony. You said that you were one of the founders of the party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was Praljak among those who participated in founding the party?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it has anything to do with this, but as you are putting the question, Mr. Praljak was in the steering committee. So he was part of the initiative for creating the HDZ. However, we parted ways with him even before the HDZ was founded. I don't want to go into this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We would have moved faster if you'd let me, but anyway, he was in the steering committee, and to make the time clear, this was while the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed, and these were the first political parties established in the communist regime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Praljak, however, did not become a member of the party. Can you confirm that he was never a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm that - he can tell you that - because I didn't look into the party booklets that were issued. He might have become a member of the party at some time. I'm not denying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, we assert that he was never formally a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. You don't know that. I will skip over some things and move on. Mr. Manolic, as far as I can remember now, as a citizen of Croatia at the time that Croatia was being created, one of the first moves, the first major political moves, was the adoption of the new constitution. I think that you were personally involved in that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there was quite a lot of discussion in the parliament and also among those proposing the constitution and experts, that there was a lot of discussion about what the preamble of the constitution should contain?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. President Tudjman personally wrote the preamble in his own hand. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were close to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, the constitution was adopted by acclamation. There was not a single vote against.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was a boycott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And in that preamble the first sentence reads as follows -- I could put it on the ELMO if I could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher assist, please. Your Honour, I don't intend to tender this document into evidence. It's a public document. It's just to make it easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you, of course, are familiar with these texts. I only wish to point out the first sentence in the preamble. This is the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. This is the consolidated text, and the first paragraph or the preamble is the origins, the sources.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you about the constitution a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you to assist me in helping the Chamber understand this. In the first sentence, it says: "Expressing the thousand year long national identity and state existence of the Croatian people confirmed through the entire historical events in various forms of statehood and the development of the state building thoughts about the historical right of the historical people to full sovereignty, state sovereignty, as has been evidenced in ..." and there follows a list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have a proper translation of the constitution into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have read this, and what is further listed in the preamble is here, and I'm sure you will agree with me they are here so that everyone will understand. We Croats did not come into existence as a state yesterday. Our state originates from the time the Croatian dukedoms were created in the 7th century. That's in the first bullet point. Then it goes on to talk about the Middle Ages, the Kingdom of the Croats and so on; all the important points in history. And following this chronology, after nine, ten, or 12 bullet points, it is established that the Banovina of Croatia was established in 1939, which renewed the Croatian state identity in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. And then there follows the next paragraph, going into more recent history, and I believe that you were involved in this because you insisted on this being included, and the ZAVNOH is mentioned here. Maybe you could explain to the Chamber what ZAVNOH is, in a few words, and why did you insist that ZAVNOH be mentioned in this continuity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because ZAVNOH was a political body, a representative body which later was transformed into the Croatian parliament. And all the decisions it made during World War II and after World War II was a continuation of the anti-fascist ZAVNOH policy. So what AVNOJ was for Yugoslavia, ZAVNOH was for Croatia. The country Anti-fascist Council of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is also included in the preamble as part of the historical development of Croatian statehood.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So both the Banovina of Croatia as the pre-war entity and the principles of ZAVNOH that followed immediately after World War II. And it also mentions all the subsequent Croatian constitutions, including from '63 to '90, the famous constitution of 1974 according to which the Republic of Croatia, like all other republics, gained the right to self-determination and gained guarantees that it was in fact a state freely associated in a federation. Would you agree with me here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you then agree with me that mentioning the Banovina in the preamble has no other purpose than to point to the historical continuity of Croatian statehood?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can anybody say that mentioning the Banovina implies territorial ambitions? Mentioning the Banovina in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, how can this witness say what anyone else intended or what purpose anyone else had? According to Mr. -- according to Mr. Kovacic's [sic] testimony, Franjo Tudjman himself wrote the preamble in his own hand. How do we know what Franjo Tudjman meant or intended, and how does this witness know? Of course we can read what Mr. Tudjman says himself in the transcripts about what his intentions were in including that, but how can this witness say what everyone intended and what everyone's purpose was in that being included? It's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may reply, Your Honours. I laid the foundation for this question. The witness clearly stated that the preamble was written by Tudjman in his own hand. He confirmed that he had been close to the president, that he was present. So if he wasn't the person who can answer this question as to whether the inclusion of Banovina means a reflection of territorial aspirations or it means precisely what the witness very carefully formulated and what is written in the constitution, then I don't know who would be the better person to ask this. If the Prosecution has no problems about their thesis with Banovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, the Banovina is mentioned in the preamble. Why is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one was what Mr. Kovacic said himself: In order to emphasise the state continuity of Croatia throughout all historical events, starting from the 7th century onwards. That's one thing. However, Mr. Kovacic failed to mention that the Banovina had its own territory, and this is what will further emerge through these proceedings. There was a territory which Banovina had. Do you agree with that, that Banovina also was -- there was a territorial delimitation? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Manolic, but using the same logic, would you agree or did you agree that the inclusion of Banovina in the preamble was a reflection of statehood, not of territorial connotation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but the territory that was included into Banovina, what was also defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I don't want to debate this, but then the creation of dukedoms in the 7th century also had some territorial claims or connotations of territorial claims.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certain. Each of these dukedoms, and later on kingdoms, had to have their territories. Now, whether these territories were firm or not so firm, that's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We don't need to trouble with others with this. We Croats could discuss this endlessly, but I'm not sure that the others share our opinion. But I think that everybody understood now that Banovina was included in the constitution precisely in order to emphasise that we Croats do not exist just from yesterday but we've been in existence for centuries and centuries.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you this. I don't think we need to go back to Karadjordjevo. It's been discussed -- it was discussed at length today, but let me ask you this: Is it true that in that period of time, in 1991, Alija Izetbegovic, president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also had bilateral meetings with Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't testify about that, I can only suppose that such meetings took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You were a very close associate of Franjo Tudjman for many years. You were not just political associates, you were also good friends. Mr. Manolic, being privy to Tudjman's policy from day one, would you agree with me that one of the principal ideas of his policy, not only in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina but also in general, was to find solutions in conflicts through negotiations, through peaceful resolution, and in principle he was always against the war option in order to achieve any political goals?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, that was the goal. Now, as to methods to establish our goal, namely a sovereign State of Croatia, was to use negotiations and avoid any confrontation in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to now tender a document which is in e-court 3D 00306. Mr. Manolic, this is a letter of Dr. Franjo Tudjman in April, after the 24th or 25th of April of 1993. This is a letter sent to Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban. I will ask the registry to scroll up so that the witness can see -- or, rather, scroll down so the witness can see the contents. Let me know, please, sir, whether you are aware of this letter and whether this is the only letter written by Tudjman to these people.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we please see the signature on page 2. Can we see the signature on page 2, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Tudjman's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. No need to spend any more time on this. The document is self-explanatory and, precisely along the lines of what we said, Tudjman is trying to achieve peace in Bosnia. The document is self-explanatory. Could we now please see the next document, 3D 00295. Just a brief question. You said a while ago that Izetbegovic had meetings with Milosevic -- or, rather, you accepted this as possible, and you must know that there were many bilateral, multi-lateral meetings between the presidents of the Presidencies in republics seeking resolution to the crisis and so on. I think that you said two days ago that Izetbegovic didn't know that Tudjman and Milosevic would meet in Karadjordjevo. Could we please scroll down so that we can see the signature at the bottom. I'm now putting to you a document which is a letter. This is a letter that we have found through our own investigation. Have you ever had occasion to see Alija's handwriting and his signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't really interested in that. I can neither confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll try to prove that this is indeed Alija's letter. In this first passage, Alija says, "I am convinced," and in parenthesis he says, "and I have certain information in that regard," and then he says, "he," and "he" is underlined -- you know, this was a message sent by courier, it wasn't encrypted -- "in bilateral discussion offer --" that he would, in bilateral discussion, offer some partial solutions, and then so on and so on, and then he pleads with Tudjman not to accept whatever Milosevic proposes. Would that be consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's first clarify this "he." I think that this "he" stands for Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. We fully agree on that. Do you agree that it was possible that Alija was pleading with Tudjman not to agree to what Milosevic was proposing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. Let's see the date. Is it the 23rd or the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We're not sure because some corrections were made, and I think this was the 23rd March, so on the eve of the meeting, before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then that would mean that Izetbegovic knew that the meeting would be held, which I question, because I myself didn't know the date of the meeting. And also, the president of the Presidency, Mr. Mesic, was not aware of when the meeting would be held -- or, rather, he knew after the meeting but not prior to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At any rate --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all speculation anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I see my colleague,

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for the interruption. Could we get some information, please, about the alleged source of this document which appears -- allegedly is a letter from the president the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the president of Croatia, written on a Europcar note, which -- I'd like to know more about this document and where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could you tell us whether it's a Europcar who provided you with this document, or otherwise how did you obtain a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was uncovered by my investigators. Later on, I will provide more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you -- was this found in a dustbin? Where was this found?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you that with any precision now. All I know is that my investigators brought it after several visits. This was uncovered by our investigators. I know that this document wasn't shown to anyone else. I would like to show you the paper on which it was written denoting that it comes from a hotel. I think my client might be better informed to tell you about this. He might know the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document came from a man who was in Izetbegovic's inner circle, and it came to us via the former advisor to President Tudjman. As to the origins of this document, this document was published in a book about President Tudjman, and we can establish through a graphologist that the date is authentic. This was before the meeting in Karadjordjevo, and Alija Izetbegovic received this information from the president of Macedonia, Gligorov, and supposedly he had received that information in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my client for the assistance. During the Defence case, we will be able to provide more information about the origins of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please clarify? Is it the 23rd of April or what is the date? It is very important so that we can fully understand the meaning of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Manolic, we fully agree. You and I can see that something was corrected here. It is our position that this was in March, but this is our assumption. You said that this is possible, this is likely, but you couldn't be fully sure about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter explicitly states that he, in bilateral discussions, would do so-and-so, and the bilateral discussions between Tudjman and Milosevic never took place after the 24th of April. So this letter could only have been written on the 24th of March, because the bilateral meeting took place on the 25th in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you are categorically claiming something that is not fully true, namely that no meetings were held after that day. I cannot claim that, assert that with full certainty. I can say neither yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm skipping over some topics. I'm trying to be as focused as possible. Mr. Manolic, is it true that the primary issue and the primary interest of the Republic of Croatia in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the early stage in 1991 and 1992, was it Croatia's primary interest to ensure that Bosnia and Herzegovina remain as an independent state and that it doesn't join some creation that at the time was referred to as Serboslavia? Was it the strategic interest of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this was in the context of the break-up of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When asked by the Presiding Judge during the first day of your testimony, on page 98, line 2, you confirm that it was Tudjman's position that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina had to organise themselves for the purpose of their defence. I'm asking this now for the sake of the transcript. I think that it wasn't clearly stated. I think that it was hinted at that this organising meant them preparing their defence against the aggression of Greater Serbia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time there was no mention of any defence against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We always have to be very specific with the dates, yes, but this is what this pertained to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, since we're running out of time, I'm not quite sure how to do this, but my client touched upon some topics today --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're not. You're definitely not. This morning my client showed you some documents. Namely, he wanted to illustrate that there were numerous examples of the conduct of Croatia both before the conflict with the Muslims and during the conflict, showing that there was no plan in Croatia to seize some territory of the neighbouring state. Let me now withdraw that question. You told us clearly in your evidence so far that Franjo Tudjman and Croatia appealed to the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to come to the referendum where the vote was taken on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its secession from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you failed to mention that an atmosphere was created in the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that establishment of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina not to join the Muslims in going to vote at the referendum. And it was very late that the decision was made that, after all, the Croats should take part in that referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I thank you for that information. So regardless of how this came about, it is clear that the voters had different viewpoints, and precisely because of these differences, the political leadership and Franjo Tudjman appealed to the Croats. They urged them to go out to the referendum and to vote, to save that state. Is that the idea?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you're forgetting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're forgetting that a bloody crime was perpetrated by the Yugoslav army or, rather, by rebel Serbs who were under the influence of Milosevic's policy, which was the crime in Vukovar, and this crime left such a huge impact on Croats that at that point in time they were unwilling to join the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Manolic, I agree with all that, but the fact is that due to one circumstance or another, and perhaps for other things too, the fact remains that ultimately Tudjman - this is simplified, of course - was saying to the people who wanted to listen to him, go to the elections, ensure a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. We agree with that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. There is no disputing the matter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, further on in time Croatia helps Bosnia-Herzegovina on different levels. Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot survive without Croatia. You and I know that. Humanitarian aid, military aid, refugees, hospitals, helping sport life. I can go on and on and show you many, many documents to bear it out. So why is Croatia doing that if it had a plan to divide up the territory in the future? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you'd have to tell me then why an armed conflict took place in the first place. Who started it and why, what the reason was. What you're saying now, we agree. We agree up to that point, and I can be -- I could be a Defence witness, I can be your witness up until that particular point. But then you will have to answer why. First of all, why were the Croats indoctrinated nonetheless to vote against? And ultimately that's what happened, because none of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the Croatian leadership had the moral force to go together with the Serbs after the Vukovar tragedy. So that's why I'm saying Vukovar was a catalyst in those relationships, and it was at that point in time that relations grew cold between Milosevic and Tudjman. That was the turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's precisely it. Even if they had reached some kind of agreement, and those were the rumours going round in Croatia but nobody can confirm that, had they agreed upon something, it wouldn't have happened. There wouldn't have been the bloody attack on Vukovar and this would not have triggered off what happened in Bosnia later on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in politics and in military actions you never have any consistency, or very rarely. So who started, who led the action? Was it Milosevic's action and operation, or was it the forces who were extremists, extreme nationalist forces who launched the action and bypassed him? I don't think we'll ever be able to clear that up, you and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think so either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please kindly slow down. [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also apologise, but sometimes in the heat of the moment one forgets that one is in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you say that some things can't be foreseen in politics. I don't want to prolong that discussion, but let me just ask you this: You said yourself that in your opinion the attack that took place during those days, the Greater Serbian aggressor against Vukovar, and you used the word --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Not "attack." "Attack" is too mild a word. It was the bloody crimes took place, and it is common knowledge which those bloody crimes were; that thousands of people were killed, that patients from hospital were taken to the execution site, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with that. Everybody more or less knows what happened in Vukovar, you described the event, but the fact is that you said it was a catalyst, the event was a catalyst and triggered other things. So you must have known about this, that there were some physical laws that existed and all that was needed was this catalyst to trigger off the whole chemical reaction. So there were other catalysts too. Do we agree with that? The situation was highly complex, was it not? We agree there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it wasn't easy to find your way in that forest of trees and say that this was the cause and this was the effect. That would be quantum mechanics, or physics, as my client would say. We don't know when what particle is going to hit what electron. We know it will in due course, but we don't know the exact moment when fusion will take place, and that is the reality of those times and the politics of those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, following the question that has just been put to you, and I myself have the same question: You told us that from November, 1991, until March, 1993, as head of the Presidency you were head of the intelligence services. So you were informed about a number of events. The Defence counsel of General Praljak has indicated that during the time of the conflict between the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia supplied arms. What kind of logic was applied here? You supply arms to the -- to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is in a conflict with the Croats. What was the political necessity here that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The times we're talking about now, at that period there still was no conflict between the Croats and the Muslims. We're still talking about the Greater Serbian aggression against the Croatian territory and against the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. And so possibly -- I did not take part in it, but quite possibly Croatia at that point in time in one way or another, to what extent I don't know, did send weapons or sold weapons to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was my intention to ask those questions with documents provided, but I can't -- I haven't got the time to do that, so I would like to suggest that these eight documents -- they needn't -- they're self-explanatory; whose sending them, who the addressees are, what they're about, it's all self-explanatory, and with your permission, I'd like to tender them straight away. You have them in your binders, I will make a list of them, and the witness has confirmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you introduce one of them, at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher then put 3D 00006 on the ELMO or the screen first, please. I know that's already been admitted into evidence, I do apologise. Put another one; 007, for example. Four 0s: 00007. 3D 00007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I think there's one that looks appropriate. That's 3D 00009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, while we're waiting for the document, I'd like to mention that the dates are in 1992 and 1993, and that's quite obvious and can be seen from the documents. Then e-court -- there's another document in e-court that I'd like to ask some questions about that. It's a similar document but not quite the same, not identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's please stick to the document you have before you, 26th of March, 1993. We have a document here that seems to prove that there has been -- that arms have been sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the beginning of 1993, were there any problems between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. There were problems and conflicts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were armed conflicts, weren't there? There were armed conflicts, and we have before us a document which indicates that Croatia is sending to the ABiH army 75 RPG-7s, 7.000 mines, and so on and so forth. What is the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no logic in trade transactions that might have taken place, with or without the knowledge of certain people, certain leaders in the state structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we have the document 3D 00186 placed on the screen, please. And to facilitate things for the usher, 3D 00002 should be prepared, the next document. So may we have those documents displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the documents that were on our screens for just the briefest moment, we were able to see that the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina working in Zagreb since Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, in July, 1993, is asking the Ministry of External Affairs, Foreign Affairs of Croatia, to allow them to establish in Zagreb a military economic representative office; and secondly, a logistics -- [In English] I would like to have on the monitor document 3D [Interpretation] [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] So the Croatian authorities allowed the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 - July, 1993 - and we can see that from the document, that the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina is informing the government which individuals would be in their bodies - this excerpt in the middle - the Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has appointed certain individuals to work in the military economic representative offices in Zagreb in the logistics department of the Supreme Command of the armed forces in Zagreb. So this is official communication between the embassy and the Foreign Ministry. So do you agree that from this excerpt the past tense was used? The ministry appointed, which means that it had already functioned for a certain amount of time. It's something that's already happened. And now let's look at the second page. On the second page we can see that mention is made of the people to man the logistics department in Split. And in the military economic office in Zagreb, we have six individuals appointed. In the logistics department in Zagreb, there are 21 names, and in Split two individuals. So official representatives of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to whom Croatia has given the instruments to work with on the basis of the Vienna consulary conventions because they all had consular passports and they had been recorded, so this isn't the trading on the part of certain individuals. It's the Croatian Foreign Affairs Ministry granting permission for that. And the Bosnian embassy is writing to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like the Court and the Trial Chamber to differentiate between what is official policy what is trafficking with weapons. You all know that there was a black market and there was an embargo on the purchase of weapons where the Croatian state was concerned. So it wasn't the normal functioning of the state. It was clandestine trading. And we have a saying which says where the mind stops, the dollar allows you to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's divide that up, Mr. Manolic. It is one thing to look at relations between the official organs of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of BH, which we can conclude on the basis of this document, because you have the embassy of one country writing an official note to the Foreign Affairs Ministry of another country, so that is that kind of document; it is the formal legal communication between two legal subjects. Now, what you're talking about, I don't want to enter into that. It's irrelevant for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I just want you to differentiate between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll agree. The other topic that you've mentioned, that's something different again. That's a different topic, how individuals procured, purchased weapons and so on. But this is the formal legal relationship between the two countries, between the two states, and it was legally transferred from Croatia to BH for the purposes of the BH army. Let's forget about black marketeering and trafficking in weapons and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you as a legal person must understand that there is a difference between legal formulation of a particular relationship and reality, and you'll have to get to reality willy-nilly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. But may I have the next document 3D 000 -- 0002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just wanted the record -- I think there is a confusion, or the suggestion that what is in document 3D 00186, which appears to be simply the fact that certain diplomatic personnel were being located in Croatia, they maintained diplomatic relations during the war, apparently, don't think anyone would dispute that, but there's no indication that that document has anything to do with the document showing the transfer of arms. Those are two separate items but there seems to be some suggestion that somehow they're connected. Unless Mr. Kovacic can show us what that connection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we understood each other. I'm claiming on the basis of this document - and we saw similar documents earlier on - and this clearly emerges from this particular document that the Republic of Croatia at that point in time was an internationally recognised independent state and that it gave permission and enabled the neighbouring republic, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, again an international, independent subject with which the Republic of Croatia is already at war, a war which in the -- in paragraph 232 of the indictment states, in an international armed conflict. So we're now saying -- and this is something I'm asking the witness, I'm asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness must be allowed to answer. The Defence has just shown you a document, Mr. Manolic, about the fact that in Split there are people from Bosnia-Herzegovina with a diplomatic passport. Now, as Mr. Kovacic is claiming, is it true that there were diplomatic relations between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, which would signify -- which would mean that Croatia recognised the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with all its attributes, in all its facets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that would be correct. That is correct, yes. In formal legal terms, that holds water. That is true. I don't know about these representative offices and the names of the people that were the staff there, but I assume that the document is authentic and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You've got round this problem in a better way than I. But 3D 00032 would be the next document I'd like to have up on our screens. Mr. Usher, or Mr. Registrar, please. 000302 [as interpreted]. No, we don't need this document. This morning, while Mr. Praljak was speaking, we saw the document for a moment. Here it is. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, would you please just glance at this document. Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, strictly confidential, Sarajevo, 12th of July, 1993. If we were sitting around the table, not looking at e-court, we would see this is a decision issued by the Ministry of Defence with a view to carrying out the tasks and assignments falling within the purview of the Supreme Command Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia, and so on and so forth, and there are three groups here, and they correspond fully to the persons we saw in the previous note sent by the embassy. So what kind of trafficking is this? Bosnia is a state. Their government, their mechanism, appoints certain people to certain positions. Bosnia-Herzegovina, same state, has an embassy in Zagreb. They inform the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb these people are going to work for us, let them do the work they're doing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the word "trafficking." You know that that is always something illegal, trafficking. What this is about is that some legal bodies were involved in the trafficking. That's the only way I can explain this. Show me any document issued by the cabinet or the president of the republic, or anybody who will confirm that this trafficking I'm talking about did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I think there's no point in our discussing this any further, but it is a fact that between two states this was something that was going on legally. That's a fact you cannot deny.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if you read all the transcripts, consequently you will see that the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia identifies himself with the issue of Herceg-Bosna. This runs through the entire material. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will now show you two documents signed -- signed by Susak, Minister Susak, on the 26th of April, 1993, in connection to what you said yesterday about funding through various channels. We haven't had time to put it into e-court, so I would like to ask the usher to put this on the ELMO. Could you please look at this document. It's dated the 14th of September. There is an almost identical one with a later date in September, and there are also others. From the text, if you have managed to read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a translation of this document, albeit done at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read out the first two paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. It's a very brief document. It's dated the 14th of September, 1993. It has the heading of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and contains a number and so on. It is addressed to the administration for finance. That's within the ministry. It's signed by Minister Gojko Susak. The title is "Order," and under 1, he says: "I order the execution of a loan to the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Department of Defence in Mostar," and the amount is 5.965.000 Croatian dinars - I have to tell the Chamber that there was a rampant inflation at the time so I cannot say exactly how much it is worth, but it was worth something - from the funds of Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and the remittance is to be made immediately to the transfer account of Privredna Banka Zagreb, and the same amount, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me when this money was paid back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this first of all: Would you agree that this is a loan, that this document creates a loan? The Ministry of Defence is lending money to the HVO, in this case in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question, does the document on its face say it's a loan or does this witness know whether in fact it was a loan? The witness just said he doesn't know if it was ever paid back or not. He can ask the question, Does the document -- Does this document say it was a loan? and I can agree that the document says it was a loan, but we don't know whether it was or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave. My learned friend is a lawyer, just like me. The repayment is discussed after a debt is created. That's normal in law. First the legal transaction has to be characterised and then we can talk about a repayment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll ask the question so that we can proceed faster. Mr. Manolic, there's a document here which seems to establish the fact that the Defence Ministry through its minister is giving instructions for a loan to be granted to the HVO in Mostar. Now, this type of document, as far as you're concerned, is it a surprise to you? Does it come as a surprise, or are you telling us that that is part of the job of the Ministry of Defence, to give loans to external entities, external parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that through the legal budget of the Republic of Croatia there was no such item in the budget. The minister of defence concealed this within his own ministry and gave this loan from the ministry funds. So in formal terms, yes, it looks like any other document in good order, but my personal opinion is that this money was never paid back and that it hasn't been paid back to date. However, this can be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, can you ascertain -- can you assert with certainty that this money loaned to the HVO was never paid back to the Ministry of Defence of Croatia or that no compensation was ever made in any way? Can you say that with certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't even know about these loans that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is your opinion, you think that this might have happened; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're simplifying things. It's not what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you the following, then: Under the law in Croatia, there is a state auditing service. I think it was adopted while you were a Member of Parliament. And under this law, Your Honours, there is a certain state institution, the state auditing service, which is duty-bound, which must - and you will correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Manolic - must look into the business books, investigate anything suspicious or out of the ordinary, and say whether each ministry used the funds from the budget in the proper way or not. This was recorded in the books of the Ministry of Defence. Nobody knows whether anyone gave some money under the table.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to convince the Court of that, you would have to provide the Court with the audit of the Ministry of Defence, but I don't think you have it because it doesn't suit your purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question or, rather, we have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I want to ask for some clarification to see if what I have understood is correct. You've said that you were head of the service in -- intelligence service from 1991 to 1993, and at the same time you said that it was President Tudjman's policy not to remain inert with respect to the position of the Croats in Bosnia, which means he had the moral obligation to see to the fate and destiny of the Croats in Bosnia. Now, with respect to what Mr. Kovacic has said and the documents we have, it would appear that there was an order of the 25th of March, 1993, about supplying the BH army with weapons. At the same time, we have a document which speaks about the loan of money from the Ministry of Defence of Croatia which is being sent to the HVO. Now, my question to you is as follows: Of course, you, as an individual who was in charge of the intelligence service, were you informed about all that, and did you know about it, and did you know or was there any trafficking with profit involved and are these two orders linked, or does it all come within the frameworks of the policy to protect and care for the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position as president of this office for intelligence was not in charge of monitoring the ministries and the cabinet of the Republic of Croatia. Each ministry was autonomous, and it was not my duty to monitor them. What was done by the minister of defence was done autonomously within the sphere of his competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Manolic, but you're not exactly answering the question posed by my colleague, which was a very specific one. The documents that we've just seen, there could be two explanations for them. The first is we are trafficking and the authorities, Mr. Tudjman, yourself, or others, were not aware of this. Or the second explanation is that these two documents illustrate the aid provided by Croatia in logistic terms to the Croats of Bosnia. So what explanation would you give? Was it one or other of these hypotheses, or a third or fourth possibility perhaps? Which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to formal things, and this is a formal document signed by the person who was in charge of this, there is no doubt. There is doubt, however, as to whether this was carried out legally or illegally. If it was done legally, then the budget of the Croatian Republic should contain an item, "Assistance to Herceg-Bosna." This, however, was not there. And let the gentleman be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is the conclusion as far as you're concerned? In your opinion, what is the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the conclusion is that there was communication between the Ministry of Defence, but if you look at the function or the actions of the minister throughout this period, you will see that at the same time he was also a minister of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina although he was not that in formal terms. And I believe it will be hard for Your Honours to understand this because of the complexity of the relations that existed. When you look at the documents in formal terms, then everything seems to be in good order according to the legislation and the constitution, but when you look into the practice, then you will see that this is missing. How can we explain Croatia sending weapons to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it was itself under an arms embargo and unable to obtain weapons? So it could not provide weapons to anyone legally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop there because we've overstepped the time. We'll reconvene at approximately 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing has resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have me all confused now. I'm not sure -- yes. I see that my colleague here is indicating something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make an oral application. As the Tribunal will be aware, the deadline for the Defence to submit a response to two recent Prosecution motions for judicial notice of adjudicated facts expires tomorrow. This is an oral application for permission to exceed the word count. The word count limit, as the Tribunal will be aware, is 3.000 words or 10 pages, whichever is greater, and that is pursuant to the practice direction of the 19th of January, paragraph (C) 5. I would like to advise the Tribunal that a joint response is being prepared by all of the Defence teams, and further that the Defence is replying to two Prosecution motions in one document. The issues raised are complex, and we would therefore request leave from the Tribunal to exceed the 3.000 word count limit. I can indicate now that the joint response from the Defence is unlikely to exceed 6.000 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber, by its oral decision, grants the request of the Defence who can file its submission in such a way that it does not exceed 3.000 words -- 6.000 words. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In order for everybody else to be able to plan their time, let me indicate that I will use ten minutes at the most. I have just two brief topics to cover, and hopefully that will leave sufficient time for other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I hope you were able to rest during our lunch break. As you have heard, I have only two more questions for you. I hope we can cover that quickly. In view of your assessment of the role and importance of the minister of defence, Gojko Susak - you have mentioned him many times during these two days - I wish to put a document to you and then we will proceed to the question. Could the registry please put on the screen document P 00312. This is a report from a business trip conducted between the 4th until the 12th of July, 1992. The trip was to Zagreb, Celju, Ljubljana, and Split. Yesterday the Prosecution spent almost the whole morning dealing with this document. Do you remember what this was all about, Mr. Manolic? We spoke about this at length yesterday. Thank you. Will you now please turn to page 9. Pagination can be seen at the bottom of the pages. It's somewhere towards the middle of the page.
