Could we see that portion, please. No, that's not it. Scroll up a little bit. I need item 2, The role of the HDZ. No, I apologise. Scroll down, please. Yes. Mr. Manolic, you can see there under this chapter, "The role of the HDZ." You can see that this subject was discussed. Somewhere in the middle of that paragraph there is a sentence that begins: "Mr. J. Manolic proposes individual persons to take part in discussions with the representatives of BH and that those people should be Mr. Susak and Juric." So these were the problems that they were supposed to discuss, and you proposed specific people who would be taking part in those negotiations with the representatives of BH, namely Mr. Susak and Juric. In view of your beliefs and your position on the activity of the late Susak, it is a fact, isn't it, that it was you who nominated him, and it was adopted. You nominated him to discuss with the other side on behalf of the Zagreb leadership, to discuss with the other side and to try to seek a peaceful resolution. Can I, on the basis of that, conclude that you nevertheless agreed with Susak's viewpoints?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So why did you then nominate him? I can't say that you nominated him as a plenipotentiary, but at any rate he was the person who discussed with the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the complexity of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I know that Gojko Susak had the greatest deal of influence among those people, but -- that's why I nominated him. But I also nominated Juric, who had a different opinion or, rather, he shared my opinion in relation to the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina that needed to be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But let me remind you, this was in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that changes nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perica Juric maintained constant contact, especially with Bosnian Posavina and those municipalities there. So he was well-informed about the situation on the ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He also hails from Livno or Duvno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Juric is mentioned frequently in these minutes. It seems that he was quite active in contacts with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I don't think I fully understood your answer. So you proposed Susak. You nominated him because there was a certain value in his nomination due to his contacts.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does this mean -- please tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that I was interested in finding the solution, finding the best solution. This is why I nominated Juric and Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. It's fully clear to me now, thank you. Now that we have this document on the screen, could we please see page 10, the first passage at the very top of the page. Now that we have this document, it won't take more than a minute. We see Mr. Susak speaking at the top of the page, and before Mr. Boban starts speaking, Susak says explicitly, "We have to seek a joint solution with the Muslims, because we're not interested in increasing tensions in our relations." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another issue, please. We dealt extensively with all of the minutes kept at the meetings in the office of President Tudjman, and I would now like to see document P 2302. This is minutes of the meeting held on the 11th of May, 1993, the meeting of the Defence and National Security Council. This is a document that we dealt with yesterday. Could we please see it on the screen? So it's P 2302, 11th of May, 1993. That's correct. Could we see ERN number 01866904. I will be reading slowly. I'm sure that you will recall this. This is where you said something following the president. "I think we have to be aware that this is the fiercest attack of the West, of Igelberg, in relation to the war in Slovenia. It has to do with our positions as regards Bosnia." So once again let me remind you, this is the 11th of May, 1993. And then you go, say: "Listen here. The Germans will come. These people will come, too, and what we will have to tell them is what is our relationship or, rather, what is our attitude with respect to the central government in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then another two or three issues that are not overly important to us here, and then you proceed to conclude your discussion, and you say as follows -- I should tell the registry that they need the ERN -- all right. It's here. Great. Could you please scroll down a little bit. Two more lines down. Yes. Yes, that's precisely what I read out. So look at this passage, please: "I think it would be good --" and this is the continuation of your statement. Do you see it on the screen, Mr. Manolic? This is the passage: "I think it would be good," and so on. And then in the next paragraph you basically conclude. You say: "Gentlemen, Bosnia may not continue existing in its current form. The only solution is to partition it so that there is a small Bosnia with Muslims."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not my opinion. What I stated there was related to the entire discussion, that namely all of the participants had to voice their opinion as to whether they supported the partition of Bosnia and should there be just a small Bosnia in existence from then on. So this is the context of my discussion. I think that there is a word missing there, because as it stands now, it seems, or it looks as though I was the one advocating the partition -- the partitioning of Bosnia. However, based on all my previous statements, you can see that I was the firmest supporter of Bosnia remaining integral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And then further on, in the next passage, you say: "I think that it will unfold in this direction. If that doesn't happen, then we will see it happen in the next stage, because they constantly want to put us in this same basket with Serbia, with Milosevic, so that they could treat us in the same way. This is what this attack against us is all about. So now we should have Croatia -- so now we should pressure Croatia so that we can reduce the pressure on Serbia, or better said, make the current position of Serbia easier." So as you have just explained to us, all the options were still open. You are now here referring to the international influence or international circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So whether this is your statement or not --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my statement, but what I was talking about is that the leadership of Croatia in that moment had to state whether it supported the partitioning or not so that they wouldn't come in this situation that I was speaking about, so that they wouldn't be placed in the same basket as Serbia, so that Croatia would not be accused, just like Serbia was, for aggression. That was the essence of what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. I fully understand that. Based on that I conclude, and you can correct me if my conclusion is wrong, that it wasn't until May, 1993, in your view as you just told me, that the situation came to a point where a decision was needed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But this is not the beginning and the end. This discussion continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. We agreed initially this morning that this was a chaotic situation, and you will definitely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would say a complex situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So "complex" is perhaps a better word. Thank you for helping me with this. So it was a situation where circumstances changed on a daily basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And now we get to what the late president said, and I think that you confirmed that that was your opinion as well, that the solution in Bosnia would not be defined either by Croats, Serbs, or Muslims but by the international community first and foremost; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manolic. I would have many more questions for you because you are an inexhaustible source of information, but thank you for your time. I have to conclude now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Mr. Kovacic just took one topic off my list, so that will shorten my cross-examination somewhat. I hope that I can conclude within this session or slightly a little bit over the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, yesterday you pointed to all of the accused, and you in essence indicated that they're all guilty of being involved in a joint criminal enterprise. Do you recall that, when you said that they were all together trying to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that, so please don't put words into my mouth, because I didn't mention a single person, except Prlic, perhaps, in a different context. Not the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your position here today, and you would like the Trial Chamber to accept -- hold on --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not position. Those were my words. Please. Show me the text where I accused all six. Go on, then, with their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you're a trained lawyer? You are a trained lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as you are. We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, so it's your position here today that none of them were involved in a joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not at all what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking him to clarify his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's beyond the scope, Your Honour. This witness is going to express a view on that, the ultimate issue in this case? I mean on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't remember, Mr. Karnavas, that the witness said that the accused were part of this joint criminal enterprise, unless you -- you have a page number and line number which we could refer to, but I don't recollect him saying anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. As I recall, he did point and said the third or second tier, including the accused, but we'll look it up on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Be that as it may, Mr. Manolic, you did bring up my client's name yesterday, Mr. Prlic, and you'd indicated, at least based on -- with respect to the Washington agreement, that he was rather constructive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The most constructive document thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And because of time limitations, as I understand it, because you've reviewed all these documents, we could find that the six points with respect to the implementation of the Washington Agreement on -- in the document -- Prosecution's document P 08012. That's where he lays out the six points. Is that what you were referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was Prlic's proposal at that point in time. You have it in the transcripts, and what I said, that he was constructive, I can say that he approached a document professionally, and it was one that we had to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, and keeping with the time limitations and trying to be as creative as I can in using my time, this can be found, as I noted, in P 08012. This is the March 4, 1994, transcript where Mr. Manolic was present, and the six points can be found on pages 49 to 51. You'll see them, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's right there. So since we can all read them, we won't -- I'll move on to the next subject. Now, my client's name also came -- came up at least in one of the transcripts, the very last one that was introduced by the Prosecution. That's D 0 -- P 01325. That was a transcript from the 27th of January, 1993. If you recall, in that particular session of the Defence and National Security, Dr. Prlic had submitted a letter. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what we're talking about now. Are we referring to the proposal made by Mr. Prlic at that particular session, the six-point proposal, or are you referring to another letter? As to another letter, I know nothing about that. All I know about is the six points put forward by Mr. Prlic at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. All right. If we could -- yesterday, at the close of the Prosecution's direct examination, they introduced a document of P 01325. This was a session of Defence and National Security Council held on 27 January, 1993. Though your name does not appear here, as I believe -- I believe you testified yesterday nonetheless you recall attending that particular session. And in that session, if we look at page 3 of the document, or actually page 2, there's a letter that was submitted by Dr. Prlic, and I believe on page 3 that letter is being read. Do you recall that, sir? And if you don't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think the question is why I wasn't introduced there, because I can see that I'm not there at that session. So I'd like to adhere to the transcript and say that I did not attend that meeting. Perhaps they got this mixed up with other sessions, but I'm going to stick to what it says in the transcript, that I didn't take part at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And therefore, I take it it would be appropriate for us not to go into that particular transcript since you weren't there to comment one way or the other with respect to Dr. Prlic's letter and the conversation, the discussion that took place thereafter. That was a question. So there's no need for us to go into that document, sir, correct? We need to make a record. It's either yes or no. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honour, earlier, as I indicated, the remarks that were made by Mr. Manolic were concerning all of the accused, as I understand it, can be found on page 9, lines 18 -- 17 to 18, 4 July, 2006, transcript, and I'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber what if anything -- what weight to give to that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Briefly I want to talk to you about your book next. I'm not going to go into it at any length because I believe one of my colleagues will do so in great detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could perhaps read outlines 17 and 18 on page 9, like -- that there will be nothing more ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "In Bosnia-Herzegovina the main implementers of this policy were Boban, Kordic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "-- including the accused here." If I could read it again. I'm told the microphone didn't pick it up. It says here: "In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main implementers of this policy were Boban, Kordic, and the third echelon, including the accused here," and as I recall, Your Honour, Mr. Manolic made a gesture pointing to accused, pointing to the box, and since "accused" is both singular and plural, I can only assume that he meant every single one of them. And being a lawyer, I'm sure he chooses his words rather carefully. But I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go on to the next subject, sir, and this is in regards to your book. When I look at this, when I flip it open, it appears that you have the copyrights to this particular book that was published in 1995. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that being so, sir, it would appear that -- while it says here that a Mr. Hlad was sort of the, I guess, commentator, editor, whatever you want to call him, it would appear that, in essence, this is your text, both commentary and the articles themselves, because obviously you're the proprietor of this book and you were going to sign off on anything and everything that was included in this text; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to answer, the book was published completely legally, in conformity with all the rules and regulations, and as far as my interviews are concerned, you can rest assured that all my interviews were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that wasn't the answer to my question, though, was it? I mean, lawyer to lawyer. So --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what's the answer, then? Go on, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I'm suggesting is what I suggested in my previous question, is in fact we don't have a commentator, an editor, doing a one-on-one interview but, rather, it's Manolic on Manolic with somebody actually just, you know, doing the typing, or maybe brushing up on the language, but in fact this is you. This is Manolic on Manolic; right? And that's nothing wrong with that, but let's call it for what it is. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are doubting -- well, as the Defence, you can call any of these people who can either deny or support your line of thinking. All I can tell you is that I signed all those interviews which you have there placed and contained in the book, that I am the author. Do you doubt that? Do you doubt that I'm the author? No, you don't?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not here to answer your questions, but I have no doubt that you made certain public statements. Now, whether they're all true, accurate and complete - and complete - that's something for other counsel, perhaps they may want to raise, but the point that I'm making -- the point that I'm making and the point that I wish to establish is that this is not some commentary by some -- someone objective but, rather, it's Manolic - that's you - on Manolic - that's you again. In other words, this is your text and you're commenting on yourself. And the reason I'm making this assertion is because this in fact is political propaganda that was designed to assist you with the following elections that were coming up. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're abreast of the situation and developments. I think you're improvising with your questions, which don't hold water. All I can do is to confirm that it is my interview, they are my interviews. The commentators can be different people. You know that full well yourself. So the commentators are responsible for the comments they make, if we're here to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on the first part, if we talk about, just to help us out here a little bit, and again, I don't want to go too much into the book, the first part is called "Who is Josip Manolic?" And if we're looking at the first paragraph - I don't want to take up too much time - but the commentator goes on talking about all of your great achievements -- it would be page 7 in B/C/S, in your actual book. Now, "Who is Josip Manolic?" Is that something that you wrote, was written with your approval, or was written objectively and independently? Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the comments were made independent of me, but the man probably used my own comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, and just to make sure I understand this correctly, if you have your book open, if you open it up, it says over here in the very first page, it says "Josip Manolic," and we can see the little C in a circle, which means copyright. So it means that you own -- you're the proprietor and you own everything that's in this book, right, including the portion on "Who is Josip Manolic?"

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in looking here, we have -- in this section you have a short biography of yourself, and on page 3 in the English translation you indicate, you know, among other things, that -- I believe it was in 1944, at a rather young age, that's when you got involved in the security service business, in the UDBA business. UDBA -- this was the precursor to UDBA, and UDBA is the security services; right? That would be page 9, although I'm sure you know your text rather well.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what is contentious there. Everything it says is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My biography and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then in 1946, apparently you went for three years to the -- to Belgrade to the Military Political Academy. Now, was that a university or was this some sort of finishing school for young Communist cadres that were within Tito's --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're distorting reality once again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- both in terms of time and correctness. Please, it says quite clearly that in 1947 -- 1946, 1947, I was in the Military Political Academy in Belgrade. That's what it says there. Now, whether it's three years or five years, it doesn't matter. Don't do things like that. It's not proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then in 1948, and you would be at that point in time about 28 years old, you were appointed to be the head of the department of the executive of the penalty sanctions in the MUP of Croatia, and you were there for 12 years. Does that sound like you were the head of the prison system in Croatia? Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the judiciary and all the other participants in the penal system. In the system, I was one of the people at the head of the penal or penitentiary systems of Croatia, and all the good and all the evil within that department can be ascribed to me during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And there's quite a bit of evil during that period, as I understand it, while folks in the former Yugoslavia and the various republics were trying to exercise their right to self-determination, the national identity, those folks were being persecuted in one way or another. Some were put in prison for being dissidents; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All those who came in conflict with the law had to answer, just as they would in any other state with the rule of law. Regardless of their position, regardless of their thoughts, what they thought themselves, but they came into conflict with the law, the courts tried them, they came to a penitentiary system where there was a regime that was enforced, and I was one of the leading people there. I'm not trying to avoid that, but I don't see what this -- what purpose it serves you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get there slowly, sir, step-by-step. And -- now, in your -- in your -- in your book over here, under this whole section who you are, you indicate that -- that you introduced some sort of moderate penal methods and that you improved sort of the conditions in the prison system. Is that correct, or am I overstating the situation in your achievements?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But it says in what respect? In respect of the training of cadres who were in direct contact with people who were serving sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And here we come to the open-type penitentiaries as the first of that kind in the socialist bloc. That's quite clear, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to conclude this chapter of your life, it was during this period of time when you were head of the prison system in Croatia when a very prominent cardinal, Cardinal Stepinac, was not only arrested but was under your care, and it is claimed that while he was under your care he died because of poison. Now, I'm not suggesting that you were the one who poisoned him, but that's what's being alleged. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, in a very insolent manner the lawyer is insinuating things about me and about some poisoning. The commission that investigated the acts of Cardinal Stepinac in prison did not take this possibility of poisoning. I was investigated by the commission. They heard me, I gave them my opinion. They heard me out. They heard out hundreds of people about that same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he was under your care and supervision, was he not, while you were in charge of the prison system, and as I understand it, you were specifically instructed to watch over and care for this -- this rather esteemed cardinal, Catholic cardinal, who was beatified later on by none other than the Pope?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see how this question is relevant and ties up with the indictment, but Mr. Manolic, what did the cardinal die of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the cardinal died nine years after he left the penitentiary. I think he died of leukaemia, but I can't say for sure. There are endless reports on the subject, because he was treated throughout those nine years after he left the prison. So this could not be linked to any poisoning that took place in the penitentiary and link that up to why and how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, after leaving that -- that job, I believe it was in 1960, then you became the head of the Secretariat of the Internal Affairs of the city of Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. To make things quite clear, the chief of police of the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the broader region as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to go into -- I want to start off with where we started yesterday. Prior to coming in here today, prior to beginning your testimony, Judge Antonetti posed some questions to you before you were put under oath, and he asked you to -- and I quote, and this is on page 42, that would have been on July -- July 3, line -- line 8, Judge Antonetti asked you: "Could you tell me what your functions were in 1991, 1992, and 1993." And then you indicate: "In 1992 I held the office of head of the office of the president of the republic until 1993 in March when I was elected the Speaker of the Chamber of Counties of the Upper House of parliament." Then Judge Antonetti asks you to be placed under oath. Now, before we go to what you said after you were placed under oath, when you were asked very specifically from Judge Antonetti about your positions, how is it - how is it - that you omitted to say that you were head of the security services at that period of time? Was that a lapse of memory, or were you conveniently trying to avoid being totally truthful with -- with the Court? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither, nor did I have a lapse of memory, nor did I wish to avoid the issue, because my entire biography is public knowledge and now it is something that the Tribunal knows about through this short biography. I could, of course, write a whole book about my biography, but this was a summary that was provided. There is no reason to hide even a minute or hour of that biography and to hide what positions I held. There is absolutely no reason for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think the record will reflect that the fact that you were the head of the security services came out through the Defence and not through you. But be that as it may, let's see what else -- what happens thereafter. You're placed under oath, and the oath that you read is: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." That can be found on page 42, again on July 3, lines 8 and 9. And then it was Mr. Scott there, the representative from the Office of the Prosecution, that led you through your biography, and he begins on page 45, line 21, with: "Good afternoon, Mr. Manolic, sir, I want to run through some of your background fairly quickly." And of course Mr. Scott doesn't mention anything about you being in the security services. Perhaps because he wasn't aware of that, or perhaps he forgot, but nonetheless, again if you go to page 46, there's -- and on to page 47 when you do answer, there's nothing there of you being a member of the security -- the head of the security services. Now, under oath, sir, you were asked to tell the whole truth. Can you please explain, why is it that again you omitted to tell us the whole truth about your background? And it will be rather relevant when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you to stick to the terminology that existed. I was appointed representative of the office of the president of the republic for state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me stop you right there. Did you know that that was the office that you had -- excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go from date to date here, but we cleared that matter up during the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we cleared it up, but I want to know, why is it that you omitted to tell us that -- you know, that little, you know, insignificant, I guess, detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I might. I think the transcript will show at that particular point, as the Court will have seen me do with other witnesses, I was leading the witness through his background. I think these were all leading questions. I think the mistake was frankly mine, and I take responsibility for not asking that question, but the only further point I'll make is if Mr. Manolic was trying to conceal that information from the Court, I don't know why he would have said it earlier because, Your Honour when Mr. President, when yourself asked the questions, he did disclose that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take the responsibility for not, when I led him through it, that I did not include that again after he had told you the same information, but that was my error, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get to that section that the Prosecutor helped us out here on, because today you were asked a question by Mr. -- Mr. Praljak regarding the Mujahedin, and you called into question what period he was referring to when you were the head of the security services, and then there was an exchange -- and this can all be found on pages 16 to 18, but primarily on page 16, of today's transcript -- and you claimed not to know the dates, and then, miraculously, you were able to recall the exact date, with precision in fact. Right? That was 18 November, 1991. Again, it calls into question your veracity, sir. How is it that you claim not to -- not to know what date you were the head of the security services, and after a one -- one-page exchange, all of sudden it's cleared up and you're able to recall the exact date. Can you help us out here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I took note of that myself. Why did you say the 18th of November, 1991? What reminded you that you actually took up your post on that particular day, the 18th of November, 1991? Did that -- did you happen to remember it, or was there something that triggered this off to remind you that it was the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was asked to determine when I took over that post in the intelligence service, because it was the time when I was relieved of my duties of Prime Minister. There was a vacuum, an interim period where I had no -- held no post in the state structures, or any other structures, for that matter, apart from political life. And then the question -- I was asked when that actually was. Then I said approximately the 18th of November, but don't hold me by that particular date, because if you -- we look at the documents, we'll be able to see exactly when I was appointed. I think, to the best of my recollection, that was on the 18th of November, 1991, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, on page -- on line 10 of this particular page, page 16, when he's asked from Mr. Praljak which period of time, the response on line 10 is: "I can't tell you exactly. I can't specify because I don't know." Question: "You don't know when you were head of the secret services of the Republic of Croatia?" Answer: "I don't know the dates and you're talking about dates now." Question: "Do you know the month?" And then it goes on and on, but we'll leave that again for the Trial Chamber. Now, this exchange came over with respect to your knowledge of Mujahedin being in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as I understand it, as I recall, the figure was approximately 5.000 that was mentioned by Mr. Praljak, again on page 17, line 12, and at which point you said you didn't know anything about it. First of all, before we get to the issue of the Mujahedin, could you please tell us, how many different services were there at that period of time in the Republic of Croatia gathering information? Because as I recall yesterday, you described your function as a bureaucrat receiving information and passing it on to the president. Rather a nice way of putting your title, as a mere bureaucrat, but tell us, how many different services were there in that period of in time in the Republic of Croatia? And if it would help you to --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, none the services came under my department. In Croatia, to be quite precise, there was the service for the protection of the constitutional order, which was located in the Ministry of the Interior, which was responsible to the minister, via the minister to the government. And I just had those authorisations which the president had given me for a period of time. More as coordinator for all this information that was being gathered and funneled into the department but which were also funneled to other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. My question was how many services were there in the Republic of Croatia at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was the internal affairs service, the service in the internal affairs, there was some sort of informative service within the army, information service in the army, and there was some sort of service, I believe, informative or information service, within the Foreign Ministry. All those people -- all those people who were in charge of these different sectors were responsible directly and formally to their ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How were you gathering your information? You were a one-person office? Didn't you have agents? Didn't you have folks gathering information or passing it on? Are you sitting here today -- I just want to make sure: Are you sitting here today claiming that no information was coming to you from all these other services?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't claim that. You're distorting things again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's why I'm trying to get you --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it could have sent. It didn't but it could have sent. Now, as far as the service of the apparatus was concerned, there were only five of us in that service, so you can weigh how -- what the scope of that intelligence work was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you were the number two man in Croatia at the time, power speaking. You were at the right hand of President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're distorting things. Where did you find this number two? Please adhere to the proper legal terminology because you're a lawyer. In the Croatian constitution there is only the office of president. No vice-presidents or anything else. The second-ranking man is the Speaker of parliament, according to the constitution, and I was not that except in the Upper House, and that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you're saying de jure you were not the number two, but you're not claiming here today that de facto you weren't. I mean, there's a reason why President Tudjman put you in that position. Most likely because of your previous experience in -- as -- in the security services.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Certainly he appreciated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course. And I take it in all those years during the Tito era, you had honed and fine-tuned your skills in gathering information; right? That's why he wanted you there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're distorting things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around this period I was a politician, a man dealing in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt the witness too and Mr. Karnavas. I would like only to say, as it was mentioned before, that we are actually -- we would like to listen to the witness mainly about that trial which is going on and about the accused or in general terms, but frankly speaking, I do not see too much reason how Cardinal Stepinac would come into the picture, and also those work of the witness which happened in the '40s and '50s. So that is why I would like to ask you, Mr. Karnavas, to concentrate, if possible, to the -- to those issues which are really before us and which are very important as far as the indictment is concerned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As you recall, I -- he just acknowledged that he was hand-picked by Tudjman because of his skills and experience in working as UDBA and the secret services during those years. That is relevant because today he was claiming that he didn't have any information and no information was coming to him, while yesterday he seemed to have all the answers while being questioned by the Prosecution. So I do think that there is some relevance to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to -- to General Praljak that you didn't know anything about the Mujahedin because you said that it was never discussed at any of those meetings. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, but I could also ask whether the number of 5.000 presented by Mr. Praljak is correct. Was it 501? That's why I can't answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But again you're playing tricks on me. It's not that I personally knew nothing. I knew a lot, but it's not relevant for these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's where -- sir --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that's relevant, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a question about Mujahedin. You had to be informed, or we had to point it out to you that you were the head of the secret service. You begrudgingly told us when. Now you're telling us that you had all those skills and that's why you were picked. Now, when you were asked the question about the Mujahedin, you said, "Everything that you're asking me now and putting to me are things that were not discussed at any meeting that I -- that I took part in," and that was the reason for you saying that you didn't know anything about the Mujahedin. Yes or no. And it's on page 16. It can be found on the transcript. You stand by your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have a single document about this transport of Mujahedin through Croatia. No document whatsoever. You're speaking off the top of your head, whether they went through Croatia or by some other route, but all of that is irrelevant for this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, we're not going to spend hours on this question of the Mujahedin. You said that you were in charge of coordinating the intelligence services. You said that there was a service under the Defence Ministry, there was another under the Ministry of the Interior, and one within the Foreign Affairs Ministry. So you coordinated this activity. Now, when one coordinates, it means that you meet the head people of the individual services, and you must have had meetings with them. Now, after these meetings or when you had these meetings, did one of the services at one point in time speak about the fact that there were foreigners coming from Arab countries, transiting through Croatia, and going to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that subject mentioned at some point in time in front of you when you were the coordinator of the intelligence services - in the plural - the intelligence services of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with full responsibility, I can tell you we did not have the information presented here concerning the Mujahedin and their transit through Croatia. There are people still alive, if you want to establish this fact, who were at the head of these services, and they can tell you whether they ever told me anything about such information or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, for example, was the word "Mujahedin" uttered in Croatia? Could you hear the word being used in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. To the best of my recollection, no. The term "volunteers from various Arabic countries," was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I do -- I do appreciate -- I do appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at the Prosecution's evidence, P 03517. This would be a National Security Council meeting 17 July, 1993. On page 17 it's the president, the president speaking, and he begins by saying, and I quote: "Gentlemen, it's very interesting what Milosevic said, that there are 5 to 6.000 of Mujahedin in Bosnia," and then it goes on to have this discussion about Mujahedin. Now, interestingly enough, Your Honour, and Mr. Manolic, if we go to page 33 of the very same meeting of the National Security Council on 17 July, 1993, of which you were a member, your name pops up. So obviously from that we can conclude that you were present at that very same meeting where the issue of Mujahedin were being discussed. Again, it's on page 33 in the English transcript. We see your name. The discussion has something -- is about something else, but nonetheless you were present. You were informed, and there is the president talking about the Mujahedin, and I put to you, sir - I put to you - that that is a total fabrication that you did not know anything about Mujahedin when answering to General Praljak's question, or that it was never discussed, as it's indicated here on the transcript earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, would you kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president probably used the term, but in our communication that term was not common. It was not usually used in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said he probably. Are you saying that you're not sure that this transcript is correct and that maybe the word "Mujahedin" just creeped in by its own, or is it that he indeed used it? Because it's used more than once.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny that he used it, but I don't recall that. I don't remember him using that term. Now when I look at the transcript and when you read it out to me, I do believe he used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the more so as there's something else I know about the matter, and that is that Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- tried to intimidate Tudjman and the rest of us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, this is non-responsive. I'm not asking you about Milosevic. I'm asking you, sir, and we just caught you lying on the record, under oath, okay? That's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's an overstatement, Your Honour. There may have been an inconsistency, there's nothing about lying under oath and that's a completely different allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about another issue, the issue of the Livno question. Do you know anything about that, sir? The question regarding -- that was discussed in Livno. Are you aware of that incident, sir? You know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday and today there has been some discussion with respect to the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall that conversation that took place yesterday and today here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that the referendum was held. I recall what the forces were and how they were distributed in that referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you aware of a meeting that took place in Livno where the whole issue was with respect to the question on the referendum and what the concerns were of the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I am not aware that the meeting was held or who attended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it as you sit here today you have no recollection that this -- that -- of a meeting by HDZ in BiH holding a meeting with respect to the referendum, particularly on the language of the referendum because the folks, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were concerned that the question as posed - as posed - did not fully protect their sovereign rights, you know, as a constitutive nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you don't know, don't recall, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so I take it you're -- you're unaware of any other meetings that took place with respect to this particular question?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't say "other meetings." Tell me what meetings specifically. I'm telling you I don't know about this particular meeting. What are the other meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall that the -- do you recall whether the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a particular problem with the way the question was posed? Yes or no. If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember their comments, but I do remember how the question was put, and it was about this question that they expressed themselves at the referendum. Whether everyone agreed or not on the way the question was formulated, I don't think that's important. What's important is what the question was and what the vote was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that may be relevant or important to you, sir, but I put to you that there was a whole discussion and there were a lot of concerns within HDZ BiH concerning the language in the referendum, and in fact, as a result of that, there were meetings with the European Union to see whether the language itself guaranteed the sovereign principles of the Croatian people within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall any of that or do you know any of that happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that preparations were held for the referendum and what the standpoint of the HDZ in Croatia and the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be. So both the HDZ of Croatia and the state institutions of Croatia and the institutions of Herceg-Bosna had their standpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I -- as I recall your testimony yesterday, you seemed to think that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not want to vote for the referendum and therefore had to be sort of pressured by President Tudjman. Now, maybe I'm oversimplifying your testimony. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your position in this case. It's quite correct that President Tudjman exerted a certain political pressure, saying now is the time for us to declare ourselves to be together with the Muslims and against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it it would be pointless for me to show you a statement of principles of 18 March, 1992, regarding the constitutional arrangement for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean, given your answers, it seems to me that you're without a clue as to meetings that took place with the European Union concerning this particular question as a result of certain anxieties expressed by Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina primarily within the HDZ, matters that would -- which were discussed in Livno, a meeting of which you know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to reply again. They didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we could go to the Graz issue, because this is somewhat interesting. It is your testimony, as I understand it, that -- or your belief that some sort of a deal was made in Graz between Boban and Karadzic. Or do I have it wrong?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No agreement was reached at that time, because the elements needed for an agreement were not in place. I stated clearly who asked for the meeting, who participated in it, and what the result was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we have all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you had a meeting in Graz too at one point, did you not, or am I wrong on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to, my meeting, not Boban's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your meeting. And what period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the 26th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Not the 26th of March but the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And is that the same meeting that supposedly Karadzic and Boban reached this agreement, or is this -- was that a separate meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two meetings have no connection. This meeting was a definite response to Karadzic and the Serbs in Bosnia that the Croats would participate in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As far as another meeting in Graz, do you have any information that might have taken place between Mr. Boban and Karadzic? If you don't know, then I'll move on. If you do know, then I have something to show you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not informed about the meeting between Boban and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as you sit here today you're not suggesting that there was any agreement, are you, sir? Since you don't know, we want to make sure that the Trial Chamber is clear that as far as you know - as far as you know - especially in light of the positions that you held and the information that you were gathering, you are unaware of any agreement that was reached between Karadzic and Boban in a place called Graz.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was known about that meeting was that some of these elements were mentioned at the session of the Defence and National Security Council chaired by President Tudjman. Something was also published in the media, but I did not know that the meeting was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you by any chance have a chance to look at the letter that was sent by Mate Boban on the 17th of May, 1992? It was sort of a letter to the diaspora. It was a public statement regarding this. Did you get a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that letter, Boban's letter addressed to I don't know who, the public or -- I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, just -- just to be on the safe side, if we could pull up 1D 00428. 00428, if we could just look at it. And while this is being pulled up, if I could just ask a couple of other questions. During that period of time, it seems to me that everybody is quoting everybody in the sense that everybody is looking to partner up. The Serbs are talking to the Muslims, the Serbs are talking to the Croats, the Croats are talking to -- to the Serbs. It seems to me everybody's trying to find a way out of the situation that everyone found themselves in as a result of the break-up of Yugoslavia. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It's correct that everybody was looking for a way out with the least losses and the least casualties and victims, to resolve the overall crisis both in Bosnia and in Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And at the Yugoslav level -- in fact, you know, you had all sorts of meetings between the various presidents of the republics. Sometimes it was two, sometimes it was three at a time, and they were rotating from place to place, trying to -- to find a way out of this solution -- out of this situation that was created with the break-up of Yugoslavia or the breaking up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you've told us about your high political positions that you've held. Can I ask you whether you participated in -- I mean, you told us that you did participate in Graz in a meeting, and just to finish that, may I ask who organised that? Who sent you to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman received a request from Karadzic saying that he would like to meet him. Him, let me stress. President Tudjman didn't want to go to that meeting because he had other obligations, so he tasked me and Professor Zvonko - help me, please, the last name escapes me - Lerotic, that's right. Mr. Lerotic, as his advisor, to go to that meeting. The meeting was held in Graz at the airport. On the Serb side there was Mr. Koljevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our side, as I said, there was myself and Mr. Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the purpose of that particular --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their request was that we should tell them whether the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would vote at the referendum or whether they would express solidarity with the Serbs, who were going to boycott the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as understand it, and we've heard testimony here, and maybe you -- you would agree or disagree with it, the Croats in -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not interested in remaining within Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is about Yugoslavia. I think we were discussing an issue limited in time, and that was the issue of the referendum. There's no point involving Yugoslavia in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we know at some point the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their position, their stated position at the time was that they didn't -- they did not wish to have Bosnia-Herzegovina become independent; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by their moves, yes, they aimed at breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina very violently, very cruelly, with armed forces that perpetrated horrendous crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, now, in your position of head of the security services, surely you would have kept track of -- of all the folks that were working in the -- in the Bosnian and Herzegovinian embassy located in Zagreb; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that virtually a hundred per cent of those folks were Muslim, representing Bosnia and Herzegovina? No Serbs and certainly no Croats working there? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me because I don't know that, so it can't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you know to what extent that particular embassy was involved in, sort of, on the various issues concerning, say, humanitarian aid, refugees, and so on and so forth? Do you know anything about that in light of the various positions that you held during the critical period of the indictment; 1991, 1992, 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia there was a Ministry for Humanitarian Aid which handled all of those issues. I personally didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But normally, in most embassies, usually you have members of the other services working there, if you get my drift, you know. So were you keeping abreast of who was coming and going and what was happening within Croatia from that -- from that particular embassy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is done similarly to things that are done in all other services. So I don't see how this relates to what we're discussing here and to your question. I don't see whether you're trying to disqualify me or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to figure out to what extent you were keeping abreast of the events that were taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because there were -- there was a line of questioning today where you seemed to indicate that you really didn't know what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you being in that particular position, being informed, and as you well know, all sorts of services working in and around Zagreb, especially from Western countries, providing you with information and exchanging information, and I'm wondering how is it that today you say you didn't know a whole lot of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina in light of your position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you have an overactive imagination when you're implying that there were all these services during this intelligence work. There is no need for me to enter into --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the transcripts - and we're not going to go through them because I do need, Mr. President, two or three days to do that, but in light of the time limitations we won't - but if we did go to the transcripts, one could see that there are some geopolitical discussions taking place. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify about all these sessions which I attended, and I can tell you about what was discussed there. I had nothing to do with any other material, any other events outside of these events and outside of the interviews that I gave throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but let me go back. If you go through the transcripts, the presidential transcripts, and yesterday you told us that you were unaware - unaware - that you were being tape recorded at the time, at various points at time in history during that period there are discussions about what the Americans want or think, what the British, the French, contacts with Turkey, Iran, and so on and so forth, and what I'm saying is there are a lot of geopolitical discussions taking place in light of the circumstances. Would that be correct? Would I find that in there, or is it in my overactive imagination?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's true, because you are now referring to the other transcripts, not the ones from sessions which I attended. Your imagination seems to be neglecting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, the counsel has just asked you a question. During those meetings, were there any discussions of a geopolitical nature? You may say either yes or no. This is nothing to do with anyone's imagination. The question was very specific. Did the security council members address any geopolitical issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the transcripts clearly reflect when each session was held and who attended it. I will gladly answer any question pertaining to these transcripts, these sessions which I attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but without talking about the transcripts, from what you remember, as you were one of the high-ranking members that was attending these meetings, do you recollect whether you, President Tudjman, or anybody else addressed geopolitical issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that one can see that in certain transcripts. Not in all of them, but you can see where President Tudjman expressed his thoughts on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed as the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before coming here today, you spent, at least by our knowledge, a couple of sessions with the Prosecutor in going over these transcripts. Could you please tell us about how many hours in total did you spend with the Prosecution in going over the transcripts, because we don't have a statement that you gave or -- other than -- we do have a summary but no formal statement. So do you know how many hours, approximately, you spent with the Prosecutor on these documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't spend time with the Prosecutor. I had seen the transcripts earlier, so there was no need for me to spend time with them going over this. But the Prosecutor would be better placed to tell you how many hours we discussed -- we spent discussing things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but here again you're not answering the question. It's not the Prosecutor who is the witness. You are the witness in the witness stand. The Defence counsel is asking you this question: Did you spend any time together with the Prosecutor to read through these transcripts? So you can say either "We didn't discuss them," or "We did discuss them"; and if you did discuss them, tell us how much time you spent on reviewing these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that I had these transcripts available to me back in Zagreb, there was no need for me to discuss them with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say you had them with you. Is that your personal archive or is that what the Prosecution provided you? In other words, did they provide you a number of copies for you to look at or did you have your own private archives? Because I understand in that part of the world everybody has their own personal archive.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. Everyone has their own personal archive compiled in different ways and means, and it is quite a hotly debated issue in Croatia, these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. By the way, did you share your archive with the Prosecution? Were they curious in looking at it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask for my archive, nor did they ask for my notes. What I gave them is this book, the book of my interviews, where you can see my viewpoints throughout the period up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to get to your book in a second. I have just a couple of questions on that. But would it be fair to say that, in light of the period that has passed by, you're not testifying from your independent memory of the events that took place in these particular meetings but, rather, you're looking at the transcripts and it's based on the transcripts that you're now testifying. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I gave my comments to the transcripts, and I gave my explanations. If something was contained there, then to the best of my recollection I would provide an explanation as to what was meant by a certain statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so in other words, the Prosecution, as they did yesterday or the day before, would show you the transcript, and it's based on reading the transcript that you're testifying as opposed to testifying from an independent memory of the events.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember some transcripts, but now, after seeing them on the screen, I remembered them. And it wasn't so difficult for me to remember them because, after all, I was actively participating in these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your position do you have -- given your position, the information that was coming your way, did you gather -- do you recall any information regarding the Third World Relief Agency, which as I understand it sort of a humanitarian agency designed -- part of their function was to get money to finance, you know, part of the army of BiH and maybe the Mujahedin? Do you recall that at all, any of that information coming your way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information, but back when I was Prime Minister, I did know that the Croatian government appealed to all Croatian emigres to provide assistance following the aggression against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but this --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to be fully precise, except for what was stated at the session of the council or a session of the party leadership, about the events involving Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But the Third World Relief Agency is tied into Islamic fundamentalists. They may not have necessarily been interested in having the situation calm in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, they may have been influencing radical elements.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such -- there was such information. It was discussed both at the sessions of the Defence and National Security Council and at various party meetings. Thus I was informed. I was informed that this was assistance going through Turkey and Iran towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. And they asked for cooperation with Croatian authorities in this regard in order to enable this humanitarian aid to reach them. Now, as to whether there was something else in addition to this humanitarian aid, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I recall reading at one point in time that Ambassador Galbraith, who was the ambassador of the United States in Croatia, at one point in time had approached President Tudjman to inform him that -- or President Tudjman contacted Ambassador Galbraith - the other way round, that is - informing him that shipments of arms were coming in or wanted to be brought in from Iran to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was asking for clearance. These events took place -- this matter came out in the open, as I understand it, before the US Congress. Now, we do know that Iran was trying to be a player in this -- during this period of time. Do you know for a fact whether that sort of information was coming through, that Iran was trying to get their foot in and were trying to funnel weapons to the Muslims, especially the radical Islamists, the Mujahedin, during that period of time? Do you have any information?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did come across such information. I am aware of that. It was discussed at the session of our council. The Prime Minister at the time, Nikica Valentic, informed that he had met with the ambassador of Iran, or some other envoy, who asked for certain things, namely that the humanitarian aid be supplied. I don't think that the weapons were discussed, only the humanitarian aid was that was supposed to be sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina via Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it also, the US was promoting Turkey in a sense that, you know, perhaps Croatia should be looking towards Turkey in a way to influence Alija Izetbegovic, Turkey being a Muslim country, very secular, and somewhat democratic. Is that -- am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. Those contacts were quite intense, and there was also some substantial material substance to it between Croatia and Turkey. And now that you've mentioned Galbraith, I can tell you that these contacts were quite frequent, the contacts with President Tudjman, especially as the situation deteriorated in certain areas. I can tell you that during those times those contacts were almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it historically - historically - the Serbs and the Croats have had their share of problems. They seem to not get along at times. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that continues to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Hopefully things will improve, but Bosnia-Herzegovina is sort of sandwiched in between Serbia and Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it couldn't receive any assistance without the involvement of Croatia, and perhaps even Serbia, depending on the situation as it existed at the time where convoys had to reach Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, at the time wasn't there an embargo on the supply of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there was an embargo. This is why I think, now that the gentleman has mentioned Galbraith and President Tudjman, I don't think that they could have discussed this, because the embargo was in place and it was supposed to be very firm. That was the position of the international community. So anything that sidestepped the embargo was considered to be smuggling, and no country wanted to be part of that, at least not publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, the policy, especially advocated by the US and some other countries, was that there should be embargo, but I also understand that there were other ways that the big powers were looking the other way as they would allow arms to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily, especially to help the Muslims. Isn't that a fact? I'm not talking about some official policy. And this is what I'm talking about, geopolitical issues.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I could say to that question would amount to speculation, and I told you that I don't want to do that. I just want to testify about facts concerning which I'm fully certain. I told you that there were frequent contacts and talks between Galbraith, as the US president -- as US ambassador, and President Tudjman, and that was true throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And getting back to Bosnia-Herzegovina being in the middle of Serbia and Croatia, as I understand in reading all of these transcripts and reading about President Tudjman, my take - and correct me if I'm wrong - that President Tudjman's main concern when it came to Bosnia-Herzegovina was having Serbia gobbling up Bosnia and Herzegovina and then having the Serbian border right at the existing Croatian border. And I'm oversimplifying it, but isn't that one of his major concerns?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a risk of that, that's true, but that wasn't the only concern. This is why our policy and that of President Tudjman was to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina in a sense as a buffer zone, especially in relation to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.
