And then within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina President Tudjman was rather firm in light of his understanding of history and culture and the position that he -- the historic position that he found himself that within Bosnia-Herzegovina the Croatian nation would retain its national identity, and any formula reached within Bosnia-Herzegovina would ensure the vital national interests of the Croatian nation within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Am I not correct on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely correct. President Tudjman was dissatisfied with this crescent border area or crescent border towards Croatia, but as you know, he didn't change the borders. The borders remained intact, and he opted for an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina the minute he went to vote at the referendum. So therefore there was no gap there, at least not in the formal legal sense, because the results of that referendum were complied with. Quite another issue is the implementation of a certain policy at a certain period in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say he was dissatisfied. Wouldn't it be fair to say that if you look at any Balkan country, including Greece, because we consider ourselves part of the Balkans, all of us have our own idea where the historical borders of our country should be, and all of us are dissatisfied with where they currently are. Isn't that a fact of life?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that your comment is quite correct. I have nothing to take issue with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, because we're dissatisfied that doesn't necessarily mean that we wage war in order to push the borders, and isn't that a fact that's what President Tudjman's position was, that he wasn't waging war against Bosnia-Herzegovina and wasn't trying to necessarily disturb the borders as they existed back then, though nonetheless he was concerned about the Serbs pushing their way towards Croatia? I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the statement that there is quite a big difference between dissatisfaction and achievement of your goals, and there's quite a big gap there, and it was never closed, and this is why the borders towards Bosnia and Herzegovina are now what they used to be before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, sir, by any chance, participate in any of the international conferences that took place during that period from, say, 1992 -- or starting with March 18, 1992, the Cutileiro Plan, all the way, say, to the Washington Agreement, which would have been around 30th of March, 1994? Did you participate personally in any of those conferences?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want you to accuse me of stating things falsely. That's why I'm trying to remember all those events. I don't think I took part in any of those international conferences unless they are the conferences with the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, unless we take into account contacts with Serbia at certain points in time. I think that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would it be fair to say that throughout this period, though, from 1992 to 1994, one the main issues with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina that all three sides are having - Serbs, Croats, Muslims - is how within this -- the geographical borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina they're going to find their own space in the sense of preserving their vital national interest? Isn't that what's happening throughout this period with all these negotiations, trying to find the proper formula?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly a formula was being sought to satisfy those interests. But we're not only talking about 1992. We're talking about the time when the question of the disintegration of Yugoslavia cropped up in the first place. Are we going to retain the borders of the autonomous republics, which the Badinter Commission would ultimately confirm as state borders. So that's when those problems arose in respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then of course it touched upon all the neighbouring states and the problem arose there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But with the break-up of Yugoslavia, if we just focus on Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have three constituent nations that are guaranteed by the 1974 constitution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, even though the Croats were 17.4 or 17.5 per cent of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not considered a minority but, rather, a nation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was considered to be the constituent element of that state which was Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's a vast difference between being a constitutive element and being a minority.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there was a difference, and that was defined by the constitution, whether you were a constituent element, which means on a footing of equality with all the other elements, or were you a national minority. And in the constitutions of all those republics, that is repeated today too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And -- and because of this -- this element, this aspect within the constitution of 1974, with the break-up of Yugoslavia, now within Bosnia-Herzegovina these three different nations are trying to figure out how they're going to co-exist, sharing the same -- within this geographical space called Bosnia-Herzegovina as it existed as a republic within -- you know, prior to the break-up.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, sir --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also, because of that, all those who had the thesis of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina meant that set-up. Not a one-party set-up but the internal set-up with equality of all those elements. And then constitutionally to resolve the question of management in an administration in certain areas, whether it would be proportionate to the Muslims, Croats, Serbs population, and then their part in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that you didn't -- you don't recall, at least, participating in any of these conferences. I take it that would also go for the -- did you, by any chance, look at the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, you know, in detail to see what exactly that plan called for in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm sure you heard of it, but did you at the time study it to see what exactly was the nature of the plan itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Stoltenberg took part for a long period of time in seeking a solution not only to Bosnia-Herzegovina but also a solution between Serbia proper and Croatia. I don't remember his exact plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina at the moment, but I do know that it existed, and I also know that it was intensively put forward as a possible solution, one possible solution for the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And if we look at the dates, because this one -- I believe if we look at the dates and the events as they unfold, it seems to me - and maybe I'm wrong, and perhaps you can correct me if you know - that the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was the precursor -- the precursor to the Washington Agreement that ultimately led to the formation of the federation within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday you did bring up the issue of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as opposed to the Croatian Community of -- it should be Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and then you -- as opposed to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Did you by any chance during that period of time study or review any of the statutory decisions which brought -- which created the community or the republic to see how they were formulated, on what grounds, what basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as a community of Herceg-Bosna existed as an organisation which was there to resist the Serb aggression, there was nothing contested in Croatian policy and amongst us. However, when it was reformulated to create Herceg-Bosna as a state, that's when the misunderstandings arose. I personally felt that you could not have a state within a state, and Herceg-Bosna had all the elements of statehood, and that is what led to the conflict with the Muslims or, rather, the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say a state within a state. And my question now is did you at the time review the decisions, the legislation, the jurisprudence, decisions, decrees, and what have you, and was it based on your analysis that you came -- your own independent analysis as lawyer, was it your independent conclusion that this was a state within a state, or was this something that you opined later or you learned later or was told to you later?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read those decisions directly. I didn't study them. But what you must understand politically is the elements that were exposed towards the other side, that is to say the state, that Herceg-Bosna pinpointed as being state elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you indicated you us that you spent very little time in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this critical period. Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing except for a session in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What year --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other situations I wasn't in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to talk about the country Bosnia-Herzegovina. When you were in Sarajevo, when was this? What period? Do you remember, about what year?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was still 1990, perhaps the beginning of 1991, when those relationships, politically speaking, were very good or fairly good between the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Izetbegovic specifically, and the Presidency of Croatia with President Tudjman at its head. So that was that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm sure you were aware back then, as you are today, that at some point Sarajevo came under siege.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't in Sarajevo then when it was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But we could all see it on CNN. So I mean, that's not a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody's denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is no dilemma, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going step-by-step. Now, we -- we had another witness here, Mr. Kljuic, and we questioned him a little bit about this period of time, and he was able to tell us that in essence Sarajevo, where the government was, was unable to provide for the rest of the country because it was under siege and, therefore, the communities outside of Sarajevo had to fend for themselves. Would you have any -- would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. I don't think it's proper to talk to the witness about what some other witness has testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on what grounds, Your Honour? Can I have a ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it is generally not proper to ask this witness to talk -- comment on what another witness has said. He can ask the question, What did you think the state of affairs was, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour. I'll rephrase. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, that question was already asked on several occasions, because it has to do with Defence strategy and, as such, the Defence considers that it should ask the question, whether they're right or wrong. Now, if the witness responds to a question about Sarajevo under siege without referring to Mr. Kljuic, the Defence can say, to the best of his knowledge, does the witness know that Sarajevo was under siege? He can say yes or no, and what were the consequences of that situation. So this is a politician par excellence, and he had important responsibilities, and I'm sure he heard about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just let me be clear. Just let me be clear on my position. I'm not saying he can't be asked about Sarajevo but I don't think it should be proper to be couched in terms of what some other witness said. Just ask Mr. Manolic directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm willing to rephrase, Your Honour, but I don't want to concede the point because I am entitled to either get a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Restate your question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us you were in Sarajevo once around the period of 1990. Can you tell us whether the central bank was working within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Say 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, do you know whether the central bank was working? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that, because my presence in Sarajevo was at a meeting. We went there and went back. That's all I did. I didn't -- I wasn't involved in the functioning of the system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But you expanded your question to include 1995 now, is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say 1995.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, the first question you asked, the first question you asked me, whether I knew that Sarajevo was under siege, yes, I do know that, or I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go step-by-step because of the objection raised by the Prosecutor. You're telling us, at least as I understand it, because you weren't in Sarajevo, that you don't know whether the central bank was functioning in 1992, 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really testify about that. I didn't enter into any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you testify what services -- can you testify what services the government, the state government of BiH, was able to provide to all of its citizens, everywhere that is, within Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period of 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about 1990 and 1991, about -- until the aggression, those services functioned, because we communicated with them on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But I'm -- I'm interested in 1992, 1993, 1994, especially 1994, because you've indicated there was a state within a state, and now I'm trying to get you to tell us to what extent you knew what this state within a state was doing, how it operated, and so first I want to start with the state itself, BiH, and if you could tell us what services it was able to deliver to its citizens, be there having a currency, being able to pay the pensions, and so on and so forth. Providing security, ensuring that they have a national defence against any aggressors. So can you tell us with any degree of certainty that you know for a fact whether the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina was able to provide to all of its citizens in all of its communities the services that a normal state under normal circumstances would be able to provide?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hasn't the witness said several times no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Am I allowed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hasn't he answered the question several times now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It goes to the issue, Your Honour. It goes to the issue. Why is the Prosecutor afraid of the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not afraid of the truth, but when we talk about limited time -- when we talk about limited time, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you are objecting and we're wasting time. On line 16, the witness said as follows, that from 1990 to 1991 the services functioned up until the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it would appear that after 1991 they no longer functioned. So the question that should now be asked, Mr. Manolic, is this: You said -- I'm going to ask it. You said that on the basis of your knowledge 1990, 1991 everything was functioning properly. There were relations between Zagreb and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, after 1991, were there problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 1991, problems started arising. But I'd like to link up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to answer the question asked by the Defence, and that is about the siege of Sarajevo. I think that I can agree with what you quoted Kljuic as having said, that it was due to that siege by Belgrade that the system could not have functioned, the system in Bosnia-Herzegovina could not have functioned due to that. So Kljuic provided an answer, the one you quoted. Otherwise, I wouldn't know. But I completely agree with what was said by him, the answer you quoted as being Kljuic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First I want --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was exactly my objection earlier, and the witness just put it extremely well: He didn't have independent knowledge, but he's saying, If you say Mr. Kljuic said that, I'll agree with that. And that's exactly the reason I objected ten minutes ago in putting a question to the witness about what some other witness said, and now we've seen the fruit -- we've seen the fruit of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine, right. But the question that should now follow is this: What allows him to say what he's just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Scott, you keep getting up, but allow the Defence counsel to do his job professionally. He is straight away going to follow on from that because, like you, he's a professional and he knows what he's just said is not sufficient. He can't rely on what Mr. Kljuic said. The witness is here to testify, so we're going to have follow-up questions, because we're among professionals after all. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should just like to respond to Mr. Scott. Your instructions allow us to present the testimony of other witnesses to -- other people testifying to witnesses in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleague. It's gone off the page, but at some point I believe Mr. Manolic said the siege of Belgrade. It should be corrected to siege of Sarajevo. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: By Belgrade, the witness said, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've just agreed with what Mr. Kljuic told us. Of course, prior to that you told us you hadn't been to Sarajevo, weren't aware. So my next follow-up question is: What leads you to that conclusion or how are you able to validate what Mr. Kljuic is telling us, told us under oath? Is that based on personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is based on overall knowledge and information that existed. First of all, that Sarajevo was under siege, facing a blockade, and second that it couldn't function as a state ruled by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you, having grown up in the former Yugoslavia, obviously must have been aware that at least the central government, many of the ministries are in Sarajevo as opposed to, say, Tuzla, Banja Luka, Brcko, Doboj, Mostar, and so on and so forth; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that would be right, yes, that they were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether all of them, I can't claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, by any chance, what -- we talked about it before, about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. Do you know exactly what that called for? The constitutional agreement.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the details of it now. The text does exist somewhere, and please, if you have the text, show it to me and I'll give you my comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that might be -- that might be a good idea to do that at this point in time. I have to apologise for not having a translation, I'm told, but the number -- and I'll just read it for you. We'll read it slowly. The number is 1D 00526. And I understand that you understand a little bit of English, and you can read English; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're going to go that route. All right. You seem to be answering some of my questions before you get the translation. That's why I'm suggesting that perhaps you know a little bit of English.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt four foreign languages, but unfortunately, I can't really use any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could -- I'm just going to look, and if we could move -- go on to the following page, please, on 286. I just want to look at just a couple of points. Go to 1D 27-

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1D 270012 at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we're going to have to work with the ELMO because the registrar has just informed me that there's a problem with e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I prefer the ELMO myself anyway, Your Honour. And I'll have one more to look at. Hold on to this for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're just -- if we look at the bottom of the page, sir, it says the undersigned are A. Izetbegovic, R. Karadzic, M. Boban, M. Bulatovic, S. Milosevic, and F. Tudjman, and as witnesses T. Stoltenberg and D. Owen. That's at the bottom. I'm sure there's not a name there that you are unfamiliar with. And by the way, this document, as I understand it, was generated on 20 September, 1993. The first part it says, and I'll go slowly because the translators need to help us out here: "The Constitutional Agreement of the Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina is set out in Appendix 1 hereto. The three parties agree that it shall enter into force one week of the Security Council has taken into accounts the present Agreement, has confirmed that the Union of Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina will continue as a member of the United Nations as specified in the Security Council Resolution 859 (1993) and has authorised United Nations support for the implementation of the present Agreement." Now, if we go on to the next page that I have given Madam Usher, and this would be -- it looks like Appendix 1, it's on page 290 of this particular document. I'm sorry, I hope I've -- just bear with me, sir, and I apologise for not having this translated. Page 290. Okay. It says here -- it's titled "Constitutional Agreement of the Union of Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina." "Article 1: The Union of Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina is composed of three constituent republics and encompasses three constituent peoples: the Muslims, Serbs and Croats, as well as a group of other peoples. The Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be a member state of the United Nations, and as a member state it shall apply for membership of other organisations of the United Nations system." Now, this was the constitutional agreement that appears to have been agreed upon at the -- as part of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. You would agree with me, sir, that at least the constitutional agreement that is an appendix to this plan calls for -- for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be composed of three constituent republics, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was advocating throughout this period. I know about it from the political talks that this proposal was on the table, their proposal that that's how Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And the fact that the -- that the Stoltenberg -- the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan called for three republics within Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is not calling for having a state within a state. There's a big difference between a state within a state and having republics as it's called for in this particular agreement. Would you not agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I understood it, that there would be three states. There would be three constituent elements making up Bosnia-Herzegovina, and based on those constituent elements, the government should be organised, both the central government at the level of Sarajevo and the government in individual parts of the Bosnia and Herzegovina that was to be organised, but not three states. That's not how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. And when you say the three different parts, that's what we're talking about, the three different republics, because it says here, and I repeat again: "The Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of three constituent republics and encompasses three constituent peoples ..." So you would have the state, and then within the state you would have these three republics --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's a mistake in the translation. It's not three constituent states but three constituent elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elements refer to the ethnic groups on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I don't know if there is a mistake in the translation, but it's not calling for states, it's calling for republics, three constituent republics within Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you would agree with me that what ultimately evolves, based on the Washington Agreement, is a Bosnia-Herzegovina with two different republics that are called entities.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that the Stoltenberg agreement advocated three republics on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have to understand what the constituent elements are. They are ethnic groups. And it's not easy to put them within borders so as to draw the three, the borders of that state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, would you take a look at page 291, Article 2 of that page. Could we have that page placed on the screen, on the ELMO. There we have it. Madam Usher, could you see to that, please. And take a look at Article 2 of page 291. I'm afraid I can't see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it but it's a little faint. Article 2, yes. It's in English again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there we have it. And Article 2 states as follows: "Each of the constituent republics shall adopt its own constitution ..." How do you interpret that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it says "republics," then I don't think that would be correct, because we never accepted republics. You can have it translated, you can have the original of the agreement, and then I can comment, but I can't comment on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, what if I were to tell you that this is a correct translation of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan? Is it possible that simply you were not aware of the details of the plan? Is that not possible?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the outset that I was not familiar with the text of the agreement. I said that. But in political discussions, there was no mention of creating states on that territory. All that was spoken about were the constituent elements on the basis of which Bosnia and Herzegovina could be built up. So this is the only source of confusion, whether the constituent elements are states or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept the agreement entirely provided that these are constituent elements and not states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we can -- let me clear up one thing. There is a difference between a state and a republic. So -- I mean, there's a difference, and that's where perhaps we have this misunderstanding, because if we go back to -- if we go back to page 290 -- if we go back to page 290 and we look at Article 1 in the constitution, and I'll read it again, and I'll read it very slowly, it says: "The Union of Republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of three constituent republics and encompasses three constituent peoples ..."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If the union of Bosnia-Herzegovina is mentioned, then this presupposes a central government, and these republics would then be parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of that unitary state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to use the term "unitary state," but I think you got it right. We're talking about a state. Within the state there are three different republics. And as His Honour correctly pointed out, all three republics are to have their own constitution, which obviously would be subordinate to the state constitution. Now, from this exchange that we're having, it appears to me, sir, and I might be wrong, that you were not familiar back then, or even today, with the contents, the actual agreement that was reached, or the plan of the -- the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. Would I be correct on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are correct that there was a plan, but as for the contents of the plan, I don't think you're right, because even if the Serb side were to accept it, and perhaps the Croatian side as well, I doubt that the Bosnian side, with Izetbegovic at its head, accepted it. I doubt that. That's why I think it was never fully adopted. It could not be implemented. It was not viable, and you will correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's take it step-by-step. First of all, you're not disputing that there was a plan; correct? That is not in dispute?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. No one disputes that Stoltenberg's plan existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you know and I know that Izetbegovic would say one thing in the morning and in the afternoon would turn around and 180 degrees say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We don't know that, but he says, "I know and you know."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do know. I do know from reading all the documents. It's very clear. It's very clear from the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not for Mr. Karnavas to testify and provide evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further, Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, and I'm sorry, because perhaps I've on my feet too much this afternoon, and I'm sorry if the Court feels that way, but this witness said 20 minutes ago he didn't know the details of this agreement and Mr. Karnavas just continues to argue him into a position when the witness said 20 minutes ago, half an hour ago, I don't know about this agreement; yes, I know there was a plan; I don't know the terms of it. And it's made very clear that he doesn't, so why do we keep putting these questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- to his testimony that there was a state within a state. The gentleman indicated that he did not have a problem with the Community of Herceg-Bosna. Then he characterised that there was a state within a state. Here I'm showing the precursor to the Washington Agreement is a plan that calls for three republics, and obviously it appears that the gentleman, who was busy with other affairs, wasn't aware of certain details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which -- which then leads -- which then goes to the credibility of his testimony that there was a state within a state. That's my whole point. He's commenting based on speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have already spent 20 minutes talking about this. The witness has told us that he had heard of a Stoltenberg-Owen Plan, and he discovers that plans had been established to create three constituent republics. This is what -- where we stand at the moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you brought up Izetbegovic, and I just want to ask you, based on the discussions that took place while you were present, and we have the presidential transcripts, and correct me if I'm wrong, there appears to be instances where there are complaints by various people, including President Tudjman, that Izetbegovic would agree to one thing and then later on would change his mind. And I'm not saying there's anything wrong with that, but that was the nature of the way he did business during those days, because obviously difficult decisions had to be made.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you're entering into what President Izetbegovic's mind processes were. I don't think this is proper, and I think it will be hard to arrive at a solution in this way. But please don't see me as the only witness to this subject matter. You will probably have other witnesses, and you need not clarify everything through me. I may be able to clarify up to a point, but I cannot clarify further --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as for this particular agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But just to be clear on this point, on this agreement, today it would appear that you're -- that you're hearing the terms of the agreement for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provisions, yes. But I know in political discourse that there was a plan under consideration by various international representatives seeking for a solution, but as far as I know, it was not adopted. It was not actually adopted. It remained hanging in the air, and it was buried with the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Because when the Washington Agreement came in, they agreed to two republics within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can call them entities, but in essence it called for two republics, and we see that -- we see that with -- the Washington Agreement calls for the creation of the federation, and then at Dayton we have Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state within two republics. Three constitutions, plus a district that later on gets resolved as a result of final award, and I'm talking about Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you are a lawyer and you understand that these are not three republics but two republics now. But this again is not the solution because, after that, the Dayton Accords followed, and they set things up a little bit differently than the Washington Agreement did. But this problem actually still exists. It's still awaiting its solution on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not going to resolve that issue but I think we've both established the points that we wanted to. A word was introduced earlier, "catalyst," and if I can pick up on that word a little bit. It seems to me when this book was written, which was 1995, by that point you and President Tudjman had parted company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By that point --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we had already parted company politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. In fact, you were with Mr. Mesic. You and Mesic went one way; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, as I understand it, and there's some -- it's unclear, but at some point when you moved -- when you left the security services and you went over as, I believe, the head of -- the president of the Upper Chamber, that was considered as -- let me finish the question, sir. Sir, let me finish the question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, let me finish the question. Let me finish the --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're forgetting that after that I was the Speaker of the House of Counties in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir, you just told us that you don't speak English. You -- now, you obviously were not telling us the truth before because you're understanding me without the translation. So "cekaj," step-by-step. We're going to get there. Now, some have considered that when you went to become the president of the Upper House, that was considered a demotion, that you were demoted.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's just gossip. That's various opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To leave the office of chief of a presidential office and become the Speaker of a legislative body, the House of Counties, that's something different. So make up your mind. Don't repeat the gossip of the streets whether this was a demotion for me or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it was while you were holding that position that the rift between you and Tudjman grew bigger and bigger. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What office? What duty? Please be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, one of the main problems that you had with President Tudjman was the fact that he preferred or he claimed that one of his best ministers was Susak and not Manolic, and isn't it a fact that that caused you a great deal of anger and jealousy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is gossip again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that people gossiped about on the street. Give me one document about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact -- and in fact, Susak had been considered someone from the diaspora who was perhaps tied in with an Ustasha background, versus you, someone who had fought with the partisans, did your time through Tito, worked your way through the ranks, and perhaps that was one of the reasons why there was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, what is the relevance of the question here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that has nothing to do with this trial and these proceedings. My relations with Susak involved misunderstandings in the political arena.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The whole -- my whole line of questioning, Your Honour - and this is the end of it - the relevance is that obviously he has some political scores to settle. There is clear indication that he and Susak did not get along, for a variety of reasons, including the fact that he had been pushed aside, being one of the founding fathers of the HDZ. And I think this is why the gentleman perhaps may be embellishing in some of his testimony. So that was the relevance of the question, Your Honour. It goes to his credibility and motive to fabricate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, it seems that at some point in time you were working in the office and in charge of intelligence matters. You left this position to become the president of the Upper House. According to you, was this a promotion? Were you being demoted, or were you being pushed aside, or was it a standard political course to follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was promoted to a higher office in the state structure seen as a whole. When I spoke about it to President Tudjman, whether I would accept this office or not, I said to him, "I'm holding this office now, chief of your office. I am now your clerk." When I become the president of a legislative house, I will become a political personage whose survival depends on elections and on being elected by the deputies in the parliament. My position therefore becomes politically freer and more stable, unlike the administrative office I had held before as chief of the president's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that when you were president, the president of the Upper House, you had been elected by the members of the Upper House to become president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was elected. But I also have to say for the sake of objectivity that it was not against President Tudjman's will, and that's very important to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we have five minutes left, because it's time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. One minute left, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, in your book - and I'm not going to cover it - I believe my colleague may --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or you can take it home over the holidays and read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. But in your book, and there is one section - perhaps my colleague will deal with it tomorrow - there's one section where you indicate, early on, at least, when you and President Tudjman are still in a very friendly relationship and very close to him, you're talking about criticism that is being lodged against the HDZ, and you're sort of defending the policies of the HDZ, particularly President Tudjman in his -- in his approach. Would that be correct? We will find -- that we will find interviews that you give to that --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even today I defend President Tudjman from various forms of libel. I do not permit things to be said against a man who has political merit, but I'm also critical when I see reason to be, and the consequences of that can be seen here today, the things that I'm critical of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course you became extremely critical of Mr. Tudjman after you were tossed out of the party, you and Mesic. You were dismissed from the HDZ, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstand things again. President Mesic was not expelled; I was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of things I said to journalists and because of standpoints that I voiced which were not in accordance with the standpoints of the president. And you can get the materials from the disciplinary court which decided to expel me from the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And lastly, I mean, it's obvious -- it's obvious that one of the reasons that you were expelled, because you are a man of principle and you speak your mind, and you're not afraid to speak in public, if necessary, and even be critical to the president, and that's one of the reasons you had this friction with Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now bringing me not into a political dilemma but a moral dilemma. I have to tell you that even after my expulsion I was on good terms with the president, and even when I established a new party our human relations were good. Now you're trying to ascribe to me personal reasons for a conflict with Mr. Susak, and that is not correct either. I visited Mr. Susak in Canada when he was there so that our interpersonal relations remained quite correct, but politically we were [Realtime transcript read in error "were not"] in a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about Susak, I'm talking about Tudjman, and what I'm trying to suggest is you being a -- "cekaj." You being a man of principle, are not afraid of speaking your mind. Would that be a correct characterisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have described me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so -- and so if we went through the transcripts, which I didn't have time, for two or three days, to go through with you, we would be able to find in the transcripts exactly what you're telling us, that you're standing -- what President Tudjman is doing, what Susak is doing, and you standing up voicing your principal concerns. We would be able to find that in the transcripts that the Prosecution went over with you and they're about to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, I simply would like to say there is a small -- small mistake in one of the sentences. I believe anyway it is important. When the witness actually answered to your question about his relationship with Mr. Susak, then - I believe it is page 161 and line 2 - the translation went on that "Our interpersonal relations remained quite correct but politically we were not in a conflict." I believe that, of course, the intention was that -- that sentence, the second half of the sentence should be interpreted that "politically we were in a conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But what -- I guess the point I'm trying to make is you're such a man of principle that --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct, that this was a political conflict, not an interpersonal one, which is what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to get out of here as quickly as possible, and what I'm implying is you speak your mind no matter where you are, and you were in -- you were in those meetings, not knowing that you were being tape recorded, and obviously you were speaking your mind at the time that we see here in these transcripts, in the presidential transcripts; correct? You weren't holding back, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes I would keep quiet, just like people do in many sessions. They keep quiet. I didn't present in each and every session my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But -- but when it came to the division of Bosnia, as you have claimed, that Tudjman was saying that he wanted to annex parts of Bosnia or carve it up and what have you, I suspect that if President Tudjman had made and voiced such -- such concerns or such policies you, with your conscience, you being the principled man that you are, not knowing that you were being tape recorded, you would have spoken up and we would have seen this in the transcripts; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't seen this anywhere, did you, namely that President Tudjman wanted to partition Bosnia and Herzegovina. You didn't find this formulated anywhere, did you? Because if you do, I'll thank you for that. President Tudjman was quite reasonable in the political sense. He was an historian. He had broad views of social problems. So he never made such mistakes. But he had some pragmatic mistakes, and if due to such pragmatic -- and it is due to such pragmatic mistakes and their consequences that we find ourselves here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I have no further cross-examination, and I thank you very much, Mr. Manolic. I hope I didn't disturb you too much with my questioning. Obviously you're a formidable individual to cross-examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you were quite unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Praljak, it is already -- what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that the pragmatic policy of President Tudjman is what led to us sitting here today. Once again, he is pointing to a direct link between the pragmatic policy and the guilt of the six people who are accused here. Which policy is it? Which events are these? We haven't heard that even though the gentleman, the witness, accused us once again, all six of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't accuse you, Praljak. Therefore, do not put words into my mouth. You know very well how the situation unfolded in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You know that I was opposed to that. And I'm sure that you will be able to clarify further this question with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Tomorrow, according to my calculation, there are four Defence counsel who wish to take the floor tomorrow. We have four hours left tomorrow. So you can share the time between you. We shall reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.25 p.m.,
